name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Maintain high expectations for those who teach the youngest Hoosiers
description: Every Hoosier child deserves a strong start in life. Achieving that goal depends on many factors, but few are more important than the expertise of the adults who care for and educate them.   As policymakers consider changes to Indiana’s childcare licensing regulations, every proposed reform should be evaluated through one simple question: How will this […]
text:
During the first five years of life, up to 90% of a child's capacity to learn is developed. (Getty Images)Every Hoosier child deserves a strong start in life. Achieving that goal depends on many factors, but few are more important than the expertise of the adults who care for and educate them.  
As policymakers consider changes to Indiana’s childcare licensing regulations, every proposed reform should be evaluated through one simple question: How will this improve outcomes for children’s learning and wellbeing?
Across the state, early learning programs are working hard to recruit and retain educators while navigating rising costs, staffing shortages and uncertainty around public funding. The challenges are real, and they deserve thoughtful solutions. While many of the proposed changes to Indiana’s childcare licensing regulations eliminate unnecessary and burdensome rules, a few warrant additional consideration.
Among the proposed changes is a reduction in education and training requirements for early childhood educators. Some would not even need a high school diploma to serve in such an important role. The state wants to make it easier for providers to hire staff and expand access to care, which is understandable. But if the ultimate goal is to ensure children enter kindergarten ready to learn, the research suggests there is a better path.
The first five years of life are unlike any other stage of development. During this time, up to 90% of a child’s capacity to learn is developed. Children build the language, early literacy, math and social-emotional skills that prepare them for success in kindergarten and in life. 
Hoosier childcare providers slam education requirement rollback

The quality of these early learning experiences is shaped in large part by the knowledge, preparation and consistency of the educators leading them, which makes decisions about educator qualifications far more than workforce policy. It is also education policy.
Early childhood educators are often a child’s first teachers outside the home. They create engaging learning experiences, observe development, build relationships with families and help children reach important milestones. These responsibilities require foundational knowledge of child development, responsive classroom management and health and safety practices.
These are not excessive or unneeded requirements. They are the basic competencies our children deserve. As policymakers consider ways to strengthen Indiana’s early childhood workforce, it is worth looking at what the research tells us about educator retention.
A recent study by the Buffett Early Childhood Institute followed about 205,000 early childhood educators across eight states over two years. Nearly half left the workforce during that period. At the same time, educators who held early childhood-specific credentials were more likely to remain in the profession than those without formal preparation.
The findings reflect what many providers already experience every day. When educators are supported through meaningful preparation and professional learning, they are more likely to view early childhood education as a career rather than a temporary job. They build confidence in the classroom, develop stronger instructional practices and are more likely to achieve kindergarten readiness outcomes.
For providers, turnover comes at a significant cost. Recruiting, hiring and training new educators requires time and resources that could otherwise be invested in children’s learning. Industry estimates routinely place direct replacement costs between $3,000 and $8,000 per educator. 
Beyond direct expenses, providers must also absorb significant indirect costs, including disruptions to classroom quality, reduced continuity of care and learning for children, increased workload for remaining staff and family dissatisfaction. The stability of the educator workforce is important because young children thrive through consistent, trusting relationships with caring adults. 
Indiana has spent years elevating early childhood education by recognizing that the adults in these classrooms are educators whose knowledge and skills directly influence children’s development. Any attempt to lower educator competency requirements threatens the tremendous opportunity for learning in the early years of a child’s life.  
Our youngest Hoosiers deserve classrooms led by well-prepared educators who have the knowledge, skills and abilities to help them thrive.

title: Alabama state employees could see health benefit changes amid ‘difficult choices’
description: The board overseeing health insurance for Alabama state employees will likely consider benefit changes and withdrawals from a trust fund amid financial uncertainty, rising health costs and “difficult choices,” its CEO said Wednesday. Changes could be presented to the State Employees Insurance Board (SEIB) in September, CEO Stephanie Azar said.  “The board ha[...]
text:
Stephanie Azar, CEO of the State Employees Insurance Board, speaking to the board at its quarterly meeting on July 15, 2026, in Montgomery, Alabama. The board may withdraw from the Retiree Trust Fund and change member benefits due to financial strain. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The board overseeing health insurance for Alabama state employees will likely consider benefit changes and withdrawals from a trust fund amid financial uncertainty, rising health costs and “difficult choices,” its CEO said Wednesday.
Changes could be presented to the State Employees Insurance Board (SEIB) in September, CEO Stephanie Azar said. 
“The board has been hearing for a long time that you’ll be faced with difficult decisions in the upcoming September meeting, and that’s true,” she said. “You’re going to have to be.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
SEIB, which has about 32,000 active members, and the Public Education Employee Insurance Plan (PEEHIP) board, which covers public school employees, have faced financial challenges in recent years. In 2025, SEIB changed member benefits, which included some increased deductibles and copays but no impact to premiums. The PEEHIP board in June approved a withdrawal of up to $200 million from its Retiree Trust Fund to prevent an increase in premiums after the Legislature did not fund its full request. 
The Legislature was able to fund SEIB’s fiscal year 2027 funding request, a $1,175 per member per month rate. It was a $150 per member per month increase from the FY26 state rate. The Legislature funded a $1,048 per member per month rate for PEEHIP, for about 104,000 active members.
“Our benefit plan is extremely rich, and it’s a very affordable plan, and SEIB is going to do everything it can, working with this board, to ensure that that remains, even if there has to be some premium or other benefit changes,” Azar said.
Even with the increased state rate for fiscal year 2027, which begins on Oct. 1, Azar projected SEIB will “be in the red” for that fiscal year based on the current health costs. 
“That’s not good at all because we don’t have a net. That’s a very, very scary place to be, and we’ve got to get this plan over the next several years not to be faced with this problem unless we’re just knocked out of our feet, as we are often with things we can’t control,” she said.
David Bronner, CEO of the Retirement System of Alabama, which oversees the boards, warned members not to “push the panic button early” because there will be a new administration and new legislators to work with in 2027. 
“What you have to remember is that a new politician coming in don’t give a hoot about the commitment to you, or to me, or the pensions, because they got elected doing what? ‘How do I promise you something?’” Bronner said. “New legislators have no commitments to old programs.”
He gave similar warnings to the PEEHIP board in June. 
“Ask the new elected people. Ask the ones that don’t even have opposition. Do you support pensions and do you support healthcare? If the answer is no, get ready for a rough ride, and it’ll be a rough ride. I swear to God,” he said. “Keep in mind that the next administration won’t give a damn about what we submit this year.”
Azar said in an interview after the meeting that there is a good chance the board will request another rate increase for FY28, but there’s no way to know how much the increase will be.
“The main thing that’s really causing the revenue and expenditure difference is the healthcare inflation and uncontrollable cost, really,” she said. “It’s hard to keep everything in line to beat that call. It’s not really an Alabama problem; it’s a national problem.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Team tasked with reviewing WV child deaths notes number of child suicides in initial report
description: A team tasked with reviewing deaths of children in West Virginia foster care have published their first report. State lawmakers mandated the creation of the team as part of foster care reform efforts.  The Critical Incident Review Team reviewed 32 cases between January and April, including 29 incidents where a child died. Their initial report […]
text:
West Virginia lawmakers mandated the creation of the Critical Incident Review Team in 2025 to scrutinize the cause of child deaths in the state’s foster care system. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)A team tasked with reviewing deaths of children in West Virginia foster care have published their first report. State lawmakers mandated the creation of the team as part of foster care reform efforts. 
The Critical Incident Review Team reviewed 32 cases between January and April, including 29 incidents where a child died. Their initial report said that the team reviewed “a significant number of child suicides.”
Lawmakers hoped to get more timely information about child deaths, particularly children involved with the foster care system, while they tried to reform the state’s troubled child welfare system.
Del. Laura Kimble, R-Harrison
“For transparency sake, especially when it comes to these terrible and tragic incidents with children, that’s why this is necessary,” said Del. Laura Kimble, R-Harrison, a co-sponsor of the 2025 legislation creating the review team. “I would like to see more information disclosed, and I would also like to see it in a more timely manner.”
A four-month-old baby in West Virginia foster care died in Mingo County last month. The infant’s biological mother and foster caregiver were both charged in connection with the child’s death. 
Sen. Mike Woelfel, D-Cabell
Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel said the work of the Critical Incident Review team is part of the solution in addressing the foster care crisis.
“The crisis has been ongoing for years, and everyone knows that,” said Woelfel, D-Cabell. “But, very little has been done in the last decade to help these poor children who are there at no fault of their own. So, sexual abuse, physical abuse, death — those things are happening with regularity to foster kids in our state, and it should keep everyone up at night.”
Lawmakers said the Critical Incident Team must meet within 45 days of the fatality or near fatality to conduct the review and share a report with lawmakers and online. 
The team is also tasked with making recommendations to decrease preventable child fatalities and near fatalities in the state’s child welfare system.   
Gov. Patrick Morrisey signed the measure into law last year, and the review teams’ first report was due this month. Earlier this year, he vetoed a separate measure that would have changed the makeup of the Critical Incident Review Team that takes a look at certain abuse and neglect cases involving children. It would have placed the team under the Office of Inspector General.
The Critical Incident Review Team’s initial report noted, “There was limited participation due to the legislative session and member’s limited availability to attend.” The team is required by law to include members from the House of Delegates and Senate, a representative of the West Virginia Supreme Court, the state’s foster care ombudsman and more.  
“I’m impressed with the makeup of the team,” said Woelfel, who supported the bill. “We had a skeleton image of it, but when you see names associated with it, they’re the right people to be reviewing this, and they’re passionate about these issues.”
Of the 32 critical incident referrals reviewed by the team this year, 12 referrals were accepted for assessment. Seven of the child deaths were determined to be the result of abuse or neglect.
The team noted a continued pattern of Sudden Unexpected Infant Death and co-sleeping deaths in infants.
“The team discussed the varying avenues of education to parents from the time of the birth of their child and other touchpoints throughout infancy,” the report said, adding that the Office of Maternal, Child, and Family Health could help. 
The Critical Incident Review Team recommended revaluating the 45-day timeframe regarding case reviews. 
“Due to the constraints imposed by the timeframes, many initial assessments, medical examiner reports and even law enforcement reports are not available at the time of the review,” the report said. “The Bureau for Social Services and law enforcement often cannot move forward with a finding of maltreatment or charges due to the lag in medical examiner reports, with delays anywhere between 6 and 12 months.”
Kimble said she was “very cautious” about the idea of extending the 45-day time frame as lawmakers seek to address any issues contributing to child deaths.
“I think that would not be a good thing,” Kimble said. “I think that we need to have it in a more timely manner and try to fix those problems if they happen faster. We’re talking about children and children in the custody of the state, so we need to be able to … take care of them as fast as we can.”
“When we’re talking about making laws or reforms that need to be made, we have to have up-to-date information,” she added.
The team also recommended ensuring mental health services and education is provided in all schools after noting the number of child suicides. 
The legislation also required the state Department of Human Services to add information about critical incidents involving children to the online child welfare dashboard. The public data page is now available and did not list any incidents in July at this time.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Fifty for 150: Colorado skiing starts at Howelsen Hill in 1915
description: Nowhere in the country does skiing like Colorado. The amount the state contributed to the nation’s ski economy in 2023 was more than two times that of the next highest-producing state, California. Colorado is the site of many world-famous ski destinations, such as Vail, Aspen, Telluride and Breckenridge. The state is home to numerous Olympic […]
text:
A woman is seen on skis in this undated photo at Howelsen Hill in Steamboat Springs. (History Colorado-Denver, Colorado)Nowhere in the country does skiing like Colorado.
 


This story is part of Colorado at 150. Each Fifty for 150 story focuses on an event that helped define Colorado over 150 years of statehood. Newsline is publishing one Fifty for 150 story every weekday in reverse chronological order until the sesquicentennial, Aug. 1, when the final of 50 stories, about the declaration of statehood, will appear.



The amount the state contributed to the nation’s ski economy in 2023 was more than two times that of the next highest-producing state, California. Colorado is the site of many world-famous ski destinations, such as Vail, Aspen, Telluride and Breckenridge. The state is home to numerous Olympic skiers, such as Mikaela Shiffrin and Lindsey Vonn. Colorado is “the skiingest state in the country,” as one local news outlet this year aptly dubbed it.
Colorado’s leadership in the sport goes back more than 100 years. Howelsen Hill Ski Area, in Steamboat Springs, is commonly cited as the oldest ski resort in the country. It started operation in 1915.
The hill’s heritage is closely tied to ski jumping. In 1914, namesake Carl Howelsen was a main attraction at Routt County’s first Mid-Winter Sports carnival, where he was billed as attempting to break his record jump of 138 feet, according to an edition of The Steamboat Pilot from February of that year. The city of Steamboat, which owns the hill, says Howelsen Hill “has the largest and most complete natural ski jumping complex in North America.”
Steamboat also says the hill “has been the training ground for 100 Olympians making over 150 Winter Olympic appearances, 22 members of the Colorado Ski Hall of Fame, and 13 members of the National Ski Hall of Fame … It has sent more skiers to international competition than any other area in North America.”
A list compiled by SnowBrains of the oldest ski areas in the country suggests the next ski area to open in the country after Howelsen didn’t start operations until 1923, in New Hampshire. The second oldest still-operating ski area in Colorado, Loveland, didn’t open until 1937. Since then, the development of first-class mountain resorts have helped establish the state as a premier ski destination for enthusiasts around the world.
Colorado’s ski industry today generates $4.8 billion a year and supports more than 46,000 jobs across the state. But climate change poses an existential threat to the industry, signs of which were all too apparent this winter. Ski seasons are getting shorter and snow quality is growing poor. Climate modeling shows the Colorado ski season could be shortened by more than a month by 2050 and more than two months by 2090.
In the meantime, Howelsen Hill, where it all started, is still open.

title: EPA Administrator calls statewide data center moratorium a ‘cop out’
description: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin called New York’s recently announced statewide moratorium on data centers an “easy way to cop out” during an appearance at the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s Infrastructure Summit Tuesday. Data centers — which house the computer servers and storage that power the internet, cloud comp[...]
text:
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin speaks to reporters following the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce and Industry's Infrastructure Summit on July 14, 2026 in Franklin, Tennessee. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson)U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin called New York’s recently announced statewide moratorium on data centers an “easy way to cop out” during an appearance at the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s Infrastructure Summit Tuesday.
Data centers — which house the computer servers and storage that power the internet, cloud computing and artificial intelligence — range in size from single rooms to massive campuses that can use as much power as an entire city. Zeldin said he’s seen both bad and good data center projects throughout the country.
The good news, he said, is that “Americans mostly want to make America the (Artificial Intelligence) capital of the world.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“The bad news is that when they think about data centers, too often they’re only hearing about those controversial projects,” he said. But Zeldin warned communities against shutting down all data center development.
“For a local community that is thinking through bringing a data center to their area, I would encourage them to ask three questions: Is the project going to make my bills go up or down? Is the project going to be a net provider onto the grid, or a net taker? And what are they going to do with water? Is it a closed-loop data center? Is it 100% recyclable?” Zeldin said.
The remarks were part of a speech centered on reducing the federal agency’s regulatory power to “nothing less, but nothing more” than what federal statute spells out.
“Every single day, we’re seeking to limit our power, but to do it responsibly to the single best reading of the law, and to help boost manufacturing,” he told summit attendees gathered in a Franklin, Tennessee hotel.
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin speaks to attendees of the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s Infrastructure Summit on July 14, 2026 in Franklin, Tennessee. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)
Zeldin announced in June that the EPA won’t set nationwide environmental standards for data centers, leaving the issue to states and communities. 
Tennessee legislators this year enacted a law stipulating that the owners of data centers requiring at least 50 megawatts of power must pay for any infrastructure upgrades needed to produce the electricity the center needs. The law also allows data centers to produce their own power without state or local oversight using equipment like gas turbines, something opponents say removes important guardrails protecting communities from pollution. Data centers can also purchase power from independent producers.
Metro Nashville Council members are considering ordinances that would limit where data centers can be located, or institute a moratorium on new projects until regulations are set. Hundreds of area residents spoke against a proposed data center project on land near the Nashville Zoo at a council meeting on July 7. Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell has filed eminent domain legislation to buy the property where the data center would be built, though this and other ordinances may not ultimately succeed in blocking the project.
Republican Tennessee gubernatorial candidate U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn also spoke against the proposed data center’s placement next to the zoo, where she once served as a board member. 
Multiple local governments in Tennessee have recently placed or considered their own temporary pauses on data center permit approvals at the behest of residents concerned about the facilities’ intensive electricity and water use and potential to cause air and noise pollution.
Zeldin did not mention concerns about noise or air pollution, particularly from gas-powered turbines sometimes used to power the centers.
Local Tennessee officials are putting data center plans on ice to consider regulations

The EPA recently joined the U.S. Department of Justice in petitioning to stop an environmental lawsuit filed by the NAACP against xAI, which accuses Elon Musk’s company of building a power plant composed of gas-powered turbines near the Tennessee-Mississippi border without obtaining permits to power its Colossus 2 data center in south Memphis.
Zeldin declined to comment on ongoing litigation, including about the timeline for the EPA joining the case.
The federal agency is considering eliminating its requirement for public feedback for some new or modified “minor sources” of emissions, which can include gas-powered generators used to power some data centers. Instead, state and local air quality agencies would determine “whether, when, and for how long to provide opportunities for public participation,” according to an agency news release. The EPA will hold a virtual public hearing on the proposed change on July 22.
The agency proposed another rule change in June that would allow facilities including data centers and power plants to start construction on parts of new facilities before receiving permits required under the Clean Air Act, so long as those building components alone don’t emit pollutants. The proposal was met with pushback from health and environmental organizations, who say the new rule would allow the majority of buildings to be completed before the public could weigh in or push for changes.
The EPA states that the proposed rule “is intended to provide additional flexibility” for facility owners and operators and the permitting authorities that regulate them to reduce regulatory burden and “foster economic growth.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: This county lost its hospital. Bringing it back is easier said than done
description: A view of Belzoni looking north from the MS-12 bridge, Tuesday, June 23, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
BELZONI — Harmony Ball-Stribling’s path to pregnancy had been turbulent, from an endometriosis diagnosis to an arduous in vitro fertilization process and sky-high blood pressure. But as her due date approached in the summer of 2021, her health improved and those storm clouds seemed to scatter.
“It was just too perfect,” said her mother, Shenelle Ball-Green, of those calm, hot weeks.
Then, after midnight on July 5, four days shy of her scheduled cesarean section, Ball-Stribling began experiencing complications from preeclampsia, a potentially life-threatening blood pressure disorder. Speeding up to 110 mph, her husband drove her to the nearest hospital 25 miles away from their home in Belzoni, a Mississippi Delta town of about 1,900 people.
Minutes before reaching the facility, Ball-Stribling suffered a seizure in the passenger seat. Her husband pulled her from the car and performed CPR on the side of the road. It was too late. She and the couple’s unborn daughter, Harper, died on the side of U.S. Route 49.
Harmony Ball-Stribling poses in an undated photo. Credit: Photo courtesy of Shenelle Ball-Burks
The tragedy might have had a different outcome if the hospital in Belzoni, a five-minute drive from Ball-Stribling’s home, hadn’t closed 13 years ago. Today, Humphreys County has no hospital, no emergency room, no urgent care clinic, and no county health department. It is one of more than 100 rural hospitals in the U.S. that have fully closed since 2005.
In Belzoni, self-proclaimed “The Heart of the Delta,” and its surrounding area, communities are close-knit, and Harmony’s story is well known. Now, her death has galvanized local and state leaders determined to bring a hospital back to the county that has suffered without one.
“It was a tremendous eye-opener for this community,” said state Rep. Timaka James-Jones, a Democrat who represents the district that includes Belzoni and is Ball-Stribling’s aunt. “It brought to light how we are so without.”
Poverty often shapes the health disparities Humphreys County residents experience. Approximately 1 in 7 Humphreys County residents under age 65 lack health insurance coverage, compared with about 1 in 11 people nationwide. Humphreys County also has the highest rate of Medicaid enrollment of any Mississippi county, reflecting the economic challenges many residents face. These disparities are evident in the county’s infant mortality rate, which is among the highest in the state at roughly 15 deaths for every 1,000 births.
James-Jones has watched these circumstances influence the lives — and deaths — of her loved ones. She said she wants to see a hospital reestablished before her four-year term is up in early 2028.
But that may be easier said than done. In Belzoni, local leaders hoping to restore healthcare services face a tangled web of policy challenges that are especially demanding for a small town with limited resources. Its story reflects what many healthcare policy experts warn: Once a rural community loses a hospital, bringing it back can be nearly impossible. 
Signage welcoming motorists to Belzoni, Tuesday, June 23, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Humphreys County’s healthcare losses
Humphreys County Memorial Hospital opened in Belzoni in 1951 as part of a nationwide hospital building boom fueled by a Truman-era law called the Hill-Burton Act. The legislation provided billions of dollars in grants and loans to build and modernize healthcare facilities. At the time, roughly 40% of all U.S. counties had no hospital. When the building boom began to subside by 1970, all but seven counties in Mississippi had at least one hospital.
But by the 2000s, many rural hospitals in the U.S. confronted financial difficulties. Low patient volumes, an increase in outpatient care, and meager revenues left many on precarious footing. Many had high rates of uninsured patients or those covered through government programs such as Medicaid, which typically reimburse providers at lower rates than commercial insurers.
Humphreys County’s hospital was among those struggling facilities. It was burdened with millions of dollars in debts, and county officials sold it in 2008 to a private company. It was renamed the Patients’ Choice Medical Center. The hospital shut down five years later after Ray Shoemaker, the company’s CEO, was convicted on healthcare fraud charges related to another hospital he owned.
“I do hope they reopen,” Shoemaker wrote in a recent text message to Mississippi Today. “The community needs a hospital.” He said he stepped down from the company before going to prison in 2012.
The G.A. Carmichael Family Health Center, located at 16463 US-49W, Tuesday, June 23, 2026, in Belzoni. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
In 2017, the University of Mississippi Medical Center partnered with the county supervisors and U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat whose district includes Humphreys County, to secure a nearly $1 million grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to open an after-hours acute care clinic in Belzoni. The clinic shut down in 2020, and UMMC officials declined to say why. 
G.A. Carmichael Family Health Center, a Canton-based federally qualified health center with five other locations in Mississippi, took it over but did not maintain the extended hours, again leaving Humphreys County residents without after-hours care. Other public health services in the county have closed outright. Three years ago, the county’s health department stopped providing clinical services, said Greg Flynn, a spokesperson for the Mississippi State Department of Health. The county department closed entirely last year, citing staffing shortages and low patient volumes. 
In the years since the hospital closed, the county has lost a fourth of its population, falling to 7,000 people, according to census data. James-Jones said she does not believe the community can experience growth until healthcare services are reestablished. 
“I don’t know how I can see us growing any other way,” she said.
‘Something’s way better than nothing’
Months after losing her daughter and unborn granddaughter, Ball-Green climbed the steps of the stately, tan, brick Humphreys County Courthouse to attend a crowded Board of Supervisors meeting.
She stood at the dais and urged the supervisors to reestablish emergency healthcare services in the county to protect other residents from the fates of her loved ones.
“I wanted to let them know at any given moment, that could be your child, your mother,” she said. “We’re a small town. Everyone knows everyone.”
The Humphreys County Courthouse, located at 102 Castleman Street, Tuesday, June 23, 2026, in Belzoni. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
She remembered the disappointment she felt when the supervisors told her there was nothing they could do. But when the board’s makeup changed after the 2023 elections, she said, she saw these attitudes shift.
Among the newly elected officials was Reggie Pinkston, who is now the president of the board and previously worked as an EMT when the hospital was open. His own family has suffered the consequences of limited healthcare access. A cousin living in Louise, a town about 20 miles south of Belzoni in the county, had a stroke in 2021 and waited an hour for an ambulance to arrive. She died two days later.
Pinkston said witnessing residents’ delays in care has made expanding access to healthcare services one of his priorities.
“We’re losing too many people in our county because of lack of healthcare,” Pinkston said.
The board enlisted several consultants to develop a strategy for expanding healthcare access and identifying funding sources to support these efforts. In late 2025, Thompson secured approximately $1 million for Humphreys County through the congressional Community Project Funding process, which allows lawmakers to request federal support for specific projects. 
The funds will be used to expand services at G.A. Carmichael’s Belzoni location in a county-owned building on U.S. Route 49, Pinkston said. Expansion plans include extending its hours of operation overnight to 5 a.m., purchasing equipment, and a possible renovation of the facility. It could begin its expanded operations by September, said James Coleman Jr., the health center’s CEO.
Establishing an after-hours urgent care clinic is a starting point toward reestablishing emergency care services or a hospital, James-Jones said.
“Something’s way better than nothing,” she said.
‘Not for the faint of heart’
Despite that encouraging first step, Humphreys County faces steep obstacles to opening a hospital.
At the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, George Pink is a senior research fellow at the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research and tracks rural hospital closures across the U.S. He said he’s aware of only a few communities that have successfully reopened a hospital after it closed.
“I can count that on one hand,” said Pink, who knows of roughly five such examples.
Communities face significant hurdles to reestablishing a hospital, including securing financing for construction or renovation, recruiting qualified staff, and covering substantial operating expenses during the licensing process before the facility can treat patients and generate revenue, said Brock Slabach, the National Rural Health Association’s chief operations officer and a former rural hospital administrator in southwestern Mississippi.
“Reopening a hospital is not for the faint of heart,” Slabach said. “Once they close, it’s very difficult to reopen them.”
To finance a potential hospital project in Humphreys County, local and state leaders said they plan to seek funding through the Rural Health Transformation Program, a federal initiative that will distribute $50 billion to states over five years. The federal government allocated Mississippi nearly $206 million in December for the program’s first year.
The program is meant to offset budget cuts passed into law last summer that could harm rural hospitals. Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act will cut the federal government’s Medicaid spending by $911 billion over 10 years and increase the number of uninsured people by 10 million, according to Congressional Budget Office estimates. Mississippi hospitals are projected to lose roughly $160 million annually beginning in 2029, according to Cindy Bradshaw, executive director of the Mississippi Division of Medicaid.
But according to federal guidelines, the program’s funding cannot be used for construction or major building expansions. Officials said the county will instead consider applying for funds through the program to support the recruitment of healthcare professionals.
The federal Rural Emergency Hospital designation is another way rural communities can keep emergency and outpatient services. Hospitals in that program receive over $3 million annually from the federal government and a higher Medicare reimbursement rate, but they cannot offer inpatient care.
Research by Pink’s team shows that many hospitals that converted to the model, which was established in 2023, saw an increase in profitability.
But there’s a catch. To receive the designation, a hospital must have been open in 2020, making Humphreys County ineligible. Mississippi’s junior U.S. senator, Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, introduced legislation in 2024 to extend the cutoff to 2014, a threshold that would have still excluded Humphreys County.
Rep. Timaka James-Jones, D-Belzoni, near the G.A. Carmichael Family Health Center, Tuesday, June 23, 2026, in Belzoni. James-Jones is one of the community leaders spearheading an effort to reestablish a hospital in Humphreys County. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
James-Jones said county leaders have urged Hyde-Smith to amend the proposed legislation so Humphreys County could qualify. Hyde-Smith did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
For county leaders, the path to widening healthcare access means navigating a thicket of state and federal policies, funding streams, and regulatory hurdles.
Some recent state-level policy changes have created new opportunities for healthcare expansion in Humphreys County. In March, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves signed legislation exempting Humphreys County from Mississippi’s certificate of need requirements, which are meant to prevent unnecessary healthcare expansions.
The exemption could make the county more attractive to prospective healthcare providers. But the financial challenges that contributed to the closure of Patients’ Choice Medical Center in 2013 remain, and Mississippi lawmakers have continued to reject Medicaid expansion, limiting a potential source of reimbursement for rural hospitals and clinics.
Industry officials expect hospitals’ financial pressures to intensify as Medicaid funding cuts take effect. The latest challenge is predicting how these cuts will affect the bottom lines of these facilities and whether additional cuts will come in the future, said Richard Roberson, president and CEO of the Mississippi Hospital Association.
“If someone’s trying to run a business, they’ve got to be able to know what those numbers look like,” Roberson said. “And it’s really hard to try to project that out right now.”
Shenelle Ball-Green talks about the lack of emergency services in Humphreys County, Monday, June 1, 2026 in Canton. Ball-Green lost her daughter Harmony and unborn grandchild due to a medical emergency. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
‘Now I understand’
For Ball-Green, giving in to these obstacles would be a disservice to the Humphreys County residents who face health emergencies similar to the one her daughter experienced.
It has been five years since the funeral, but Ball-Green remembers it clearly.
Harmony Ball-Stribling in a 2021 photograph. Credit: Photo courtesy of Shenelle Ball-Burks

The day was stormy, but attendees brightened the gathering by wearing yellow, Ball-Stribling’s favorite color.

As friends and family gathered to pay their respects, her mother thought back on a relative’s funeral four months earlier. At that service, Ball-Stribling sang the gospel classic “You Are My Strength” to a roomful of mourners.
“She was singing, and she looked at me,” Ball-Green said, describing a peaceful but eerie expression on her daughter’s face in that moment — a sign of something to come, though she didn’t yet know what. “She turned around, and it was just that look, you know?”
Months later, as she sat at her daughter’s funeral, she began to interpret the foreboding glance differently. She came to believe it was a sign that Ball-Stribling’s gift for helping others by sharing her story would not end with her death.
That purpose had taken shape years earlier in her work as a teacher and continued as she shared candid social media posts about her fertility struggles and IVF journey in the final months of her life. Ball-Green said the community became deeply invested in her and Harper’s story.
In the years since, this gift has endured, she said. Ball-Stribling’s story has continued to resonate throughout Humphreys County, serving as a reminder of what residents stand to lose if they do not reopen the hospital. 
“I think back on when she looked back at me,” Ball Green said. “Now I understand.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Waste, fraud, abuse… and the politics of power
description: One of the oldest tricks in politics is knowing when to use a number and when to use a percentage.  If you want something to sound enormous, you use the raw number. If you want it to sound insignificant, you use the percentage. Politicians, statisticians and public relations strategists know this. Every citizen should understand […]
text:
Memphis Republican Sen. Brent Taylor holds a copy of an audit of Memphis-Shelby County Schools performed by the Tennessee Comptroller's office. The legislature voted to create a state-controlled board to oversee the school system following the audit. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)One of the oldest tricks in politics is knowing when to use a number and when to use a percentage. 
If you want something to sound enormous, you use the raw number. If you want it to sound insignificant, you use the percentage. Politicians, statisticians and public relations strategists know this. Every citizen should understand it because statistics, by themselves, are neither objective nor dishonest. They are rhetorical. They frame the story before the facts are ever debated.
The recent forensic audit of Memphis-Shelby County Schools illustrates the point. The Tennessee Comptroller identified approximately $54.2 million in transactions consistent with evidence of potential fraud, waste, or abuse, along with another $65.1 million involving apparent noncompliance with district policies and procedures. 
Those findings deserve serious attention. If public funds have been misused or laws have been broken, accountability should follow. That principle is fundamental to any healthy democracy.
What caught my attention, however, was not simply the findings themselves but what happened almost immediately afterward. Public debate shifted from questions of accountability to questions of authority. 
Buried within the Comptroller’s release was a sentence with far-reaching implications: “The largest area of concern involved procurement and contracting.” That observation matters because procurement is not merely about purchasing goods and services. It determines who receives public contracts, who builds wealth, who creates jobs, and who develops the economic relationships that ultimately shape political influence. 
Tennessee releases final results of Memphis schools forensic audit

A school district with an annual budget approaching $2 billion is not merely an educational institution. It is one of the largest public economic engines in Tennessee.
The real question, then, is not simply whether corruption should be investigated.
The more important question is what happens after the investigation. Who gains authority? Who loses it? Who inherits public confidence? Who assumes control over institutions, contracts and budgets? Those questions often tell us as much about a political moment as the allegations themselves.
Equal justice requires equal standards.
This is not a new phenomenon. Tennessee has a long history of highly public anti-corruption campaigns, from Operation Rocky Top to Tennessee Waltz and, more recently, investigations involving several elected officials across Shelby County. Some exposed genuine criminal conduct. Others remain the subject of ongoing legal proceedings or public debate. 
My concern is the political consequences that often follow these moments and the selective ways they are narrated, amplified, and ultimately used.
Corruption should always be investigated. Corruption should never be instrumentalized. There is a profound difference between pursuing justice and weaponizing the language of justice. 
When allegations of waste, fraud, and abuse become the principal justification for diminishing local democratic authority, expanding state control over Black-led institutions or reshaping who exercises influence over billions of public dollars, citizens have every right — and responsibility — to examine not only the allegations themselves but also the governmental objectives that emerge in their wake. The politics of anti-corruption can become a mechanism of governance and a tool of political calculus through which one party consolidates power when it cannot reliably secure that power through persuasion alone.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Equal justice requires equal standards.
What makes this dynamic especially troubling is its inconsistency. It’s difficult to ignore tha former State Sen. Brian Kelsey of Germantown was convicted in federal court and ultimately received a presidential pardon. Former President Donald Trump remains the dominant figure in the Republican Party despite his criminal convictions. No one in our current Tennessee GOP has denounced or demonized them. Neither has become a symbol of institutional decay within today’s Tennessee Republican political rhetoric. (Kelsey even got a “welcome home” party from his short stay in federal prison).  
By contrast, Democratic officeholders (and particularly Black Democratic officeholders) often find themselves tried twice: once through the legal process and again through a public narrative in which allegations alone become sufficient to delegitimize not only individuals but the institutions they represent. Whether any particular official is guilty is a matter for the courts. Whether accountability is being applied with equal political force is a question for all of us.
Political accountability loses its moral authority when it appears to be administered selectively.
Democrats, however, should not mistake this observation for an excuse to abandon self-examination. Too often they have redirected their energy toward one another while neglecting the larger structural challenges confronting democracy in Tennessee. Racially discriminatory redistricting, voter suppression efforts, school takeovers and the steady centralization of state authority have advanced while we engaged in political friendly fire that weakened our own governing capacity. 
Black folks cannot afford to confuse internal rivalry with strategic vision.
The answer to selective accountability is not selective accountability in return. It is greater political education, deeper civic engagement, sustained voter empowerment and higher voter participation. 
A healthy democracy requires more than prosecutors and auditors. It requires an informed public capable of distinguishing between accountability that strengthens democratic institutions and political theater that quietly rearranges them.
History teaches that power rarely announces itself as power.
More often, it arrives wrapped in the language of virtue. That is why the task before us is not simply to demand accountability from public officials. It is to remain accountable to democracy itself.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Poor CHOOSE Act standards mean squandered taxpayer dollars
description: Summertime is fading. Not in the sense that we can expect crisp fall days any time soon, of course — we will be sweating our tails off for the foreseeable future. But summer as it’s measured in the waxing and waning of the school calendar is indeed winding down. In a few weeks, when Alabama’s […]
text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake City, Utah, on March 12, 2024. More than 34,000 Alabama students receive funds from the CHOOSE Act, which pays for nonpublic education expenses, including private school tuition and homeschooling. (Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)Summertime is fading. Not in the sense that we can expect crisp fall days any time soon, of course — we will be sweating our tails off for the foreseeable future. But summer as it’s measured in the waxing and waning of the school calendar is indeed winding down.
In a few weeks, when Alabama’s K-12 students dust the beach sand from their feet and shuffle back into the classroom, more than 34,000 of their cohort will find themselves uplifted by a financial gift from the state: either $7,000 for school tuition (overwhelmingly at private schools) or $2,000 for homeschool materials, totaling more than $174 million in public funds. It’s equivalent to about 1.7% of the state’s 2027 education budget.
These are the lucky kids who applied for and were accepted into the CHOOSE Act program for 2026-27. This is the program’s second year, and also the last year that it includes a household income cap. If state lawmakers keep generously funding it — which they seem eager to do — next year ordinary taxpayers will chip in toward millionaires’ private school tuition. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Kay Ivey has pointed to the rising number of CHOOSE Act applications as evidence of the program’s popularity. 
Of course it’s popular. Who wouldn’t want free money? 
I’m certainly not going to begrudge any family a good education, whether they find it at a public school, private school, or homeschool. Every family has to find their own way. But underneath Ivey’s veneer of goodwill, it looks for all the world as though the CHOOSE Act is simply a convenient vehicle for lawmakers to rob public schools in order to fund minimally regulated Christian ones. 
The reality becomes inescapable if you review the list of participating schools: 79% of the private schools are Christian institutions. They come in every flavor, from Episcopal prep schools to Bible-loving, born-again Baptist schools. 
Mixing religion and education opens a Pandora’s box of conflicts that would not fly at a public school, from institutionalized discrimination against LGBTQ people to the kind of wackadoodle classroom instruction that pops up when science and Biblical literalism collide.
There are superficial measures in place to ensure that children are getting a quality education. For a school to become a CHOOSE Act participant, for example, it must either be accredited or pinky promise that it’s working on becoming accredited. 
But don’t let that fool you; not all accrediting bodies are created equal.
The state administrative code for the CHOOSE Act names two religious associations on the short list of approved accreditors. Both of them — the Alabama Christian Education Association (ACEA) and the American Association of Christian Schools (AACS) — push young Earth creationism, which asserts that God created the Earth in six days a mere 6,000 years ago, give or take. 
The AACS holds schools strictly to that line, requiring that each school they accredit be in harmony with the association’s statement of faith. The schools must teach young Earth creationism; school staff must affirm and support it; and curriculum choices must not deviate from it. 
Creationism leaks out into other areas of the CHOOSE Act, too. Several approved vendors on the list of classroom material providers specialize in creationist “science.” Among them: Apologia, BJU Press, Master Books, and Berean Builders Publishing. AL.com’s Rebecca Griesbach took a deep dive late last year into the CHOOSE Act’s myriad curriculum shortcomings.
If parents believe that the dinosaurs roamed the Earth alongside humans 6,000 years ago, it’s their prerogative to teach their kids as they see fit. But taxpayers shouldn’t cover the cost.
To be fair, in addition to the shaky accreditation provision, schools in the program must also conduct standardized testing once a year and report the results to the state. But they don’t have to hit a minimum achievement level; they just have to conduct the tests. Microschools — those with fewer than 20 students — are exempt from reporting their scores. (The list of participating schools includes 15 that identify as microschools.)
That’s about as deep as the scrutiny goes. If you run a microschool that’s “working on” becoming accredited, you pretty much just need a pulse, an address, a clean background check and a bank account, and you’re in. 
Politicians have tried to keep their hands clean from accountability, arguing that it’s the parents’ job to vet schools, not the state’s. And I have to hand it to them; they’ve committed to the bit, setting up the system so that no actual educators can meddle with it. 
The program is administered not by the State Department of Education, but by the Alabama Department of Revenue (ALDOR). ALDOR has done about as good a job as you could expect. They’re experts at handling money, not so great at vetting education providers. 
Ten of the 307 schools on their approved list don’t even appear to have websites.
Believe me, I’ve Googled the heck out of them. I think they do exist — I’ve found bits and pieces of evidence online — but either they’ve never bothered to put together a website, or they’ve let their subscriptions lapse. 
Another link on ALDOR’s list took me not to a school website, but to a sketchy website for a Russian casino. 
Having spent the better part of a week up to my neck in this stuff, I would like to request that we raise the bar at least an inch off the floor.
If the state of Alabama is indeed so flush with cash that our public schools couldn’t possibly use another cent, I think it’s reasonable to require some vetting of the private schools to which lawmakers are pushing excess funds. 
Approving anyone who’s capable of filling out an online form is a dereliction of duty. If a private school isn’t held to the same standards we hold for our public schools, there’s no reason on Earth — all 4.5 billion years of it — we should give them any of our hard-earned money.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia can reduce recidivism — Virginia shows how
description: Despite spending billions of taxpayer dollars on incarceration, many states continue to struggle with high recidivism rates.
text:
Virginia recently reported a three-year recidivism rate of just 17.6% — the lowest in the United States among states reporting comparable data. (Getty Images) For decades, America’s response to crime has largely been measured by the number of prison beds it could fill. Politicians competed to be “tough on crime,” while correctional systems focused on punishment rather than rehabilitation. Yet, despite spending billions of taxpayer dollars on incarceration, many states continue to struggle with high recidivism rates and revolving prison doors.
Virginia offers a different model. One that other states should consider replicating.
The Commonwealth’s Community Corrections Alternative Program has quietly become one of the most successful correctional initiatives in the nation. Rather than simply warehousing nonviolent offenders, CCAP combines intensive substance-abuse treatment, cognitive behavioral programming, educational opportunities, vocational training, accountability and structured reentry planning. Participants live in a highly regimented residential environment designed not merely to punish past behavior, but to change future outcomes.
The results speak for themselves.
Virginia recently reported a three-year recidivism rate of just 17.6% — the lowest in the United States among states reporting comparable data. Virginia has maintained either the lowest or second-lowest recidivism rate in the nation for more than a decade. These results reflect a sustained pattern of success driven by evidence-based correctional practices and meaningful investment in rehabilitation.
Even more compelling are the outcomes for CCAP participants themselves.
According to Virginia Department of Corrections data, individuals who successfully complete CCAP recidivate at dramatically lower rates than those who fail to complete the program. Three years after release, only about 35% of CCAP graduates had returned to incarceration, compared with more than 52% of non-graduates. The gap is even more striking during the first six months after release, when graduates reoffend at only a fraction of the rate of those who fail the program.
These numbers matter because they represent real people, families and communities.
Every offender who successfully reintegrates into society means one fewer victim, one fewer prosecution, one fewer prison bed occupied, and one more taxpayer contributing to the workforce. Public safety is not diminished when rehabilitation works. Public safety is strengthened.
West Virginia, in particular, should pay close attention.
Like many Appalachian states, West Virginia faces challenges involving substance abuse, addiction-driven crime, workforce shortages and correctional costs. While the state’s correctional system has made progress, it continues to confront the same question facing every state: How do we reduce crime after an offender leaves custody?
The answer cannot simply be longer prison sentences. Most incarcerated individuals will eventually return home. The real question is whether they return with the tools necessary to succeed.
Virginia’s experience demonstrates that treatment, education, job training and accountability can produce measurable improvements in public safety. CCAP graduates leave with stronger coping skills, improved employability, better decision-making abilities and greater access to support systems. They are not merely released; they are prepared.
Critics may argue that rehabilitation programs are expensive. But incarceration is expensive as well. Housing an inmate for years costs taxpayers far more than providing targeted treatment and reentry services that reduce future incarceration. Every avoided arrest, prosecution and prison sentence generates savings that benefit taxpayers and communities.
Others may contend that programs like CCAP are too lenient, but that criticism misunderstands the nature of the program. CCAP is not a shortcut or a free pass. Participants live under strict supervision, complete demanding treatment requirements, submit to testing and monitoring, and face removal if they fail to comply. Accountability remains central to the model, but it is paired with rehabilitation rather than punishment alone.
The debate over criminal justice policy too often becomes polarized between those advocating punishment and those advocating leniency. Virginia’s CCAP model demonstrates that this is a false choice. States can hold offenders accountable while simultaneously reducing future crime.
That should be the ultimate goal of any correctional system.
West Virginia and other states do not need to reinvent the wheel. Virginia has already built a successful blueprint. The data is available, the outcomes are measurable, and the benefits to public safety are clear.
The question is no longer whether programs like CCAP can work, but how many states are willing to follow the evidence?
If our objective is safer communities rather than simply larger prison populations, Virginia’s success offers a lesson worth embracing.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Summer learning works. So, why can’t more kids access it?
description: Summer is a break for kids, but a challenge for families looking to keep them "fed, safe and engaged," and the "summer slide" threatens the state's educational goals. That's why Ellie Mitchell and Brodrick Clarke say we must push for accessible summer programming.
text:
Summer is a break for kids, but a challenge for families looking to keep them "fed, safe and engaged," and for educators hoping to prevent the "summer slide" of learning at the state strives for ambitious educational goals. (Photo by smolaw11/Stock.adobe.com)Summer can be a magical time in a young person’s life. The daily burdens and stress of the school year lift, the days grow longer and sunnier, and in Maryland, the ubiquitous snowball stands reopen for the season.
Along with the freedom that summer provides comes a set of tensions that nearly every family faces. Where will the kids go? What will they do? How can we keep kids fed, safe and engaged?
Summer learning opportunities offer critical supports. When done right, summer programs are the places where kids discover hidden talents, open doors to new worlds, meet new friends, gain mentors, and build lasting memories.
Many young people rely on school meal programs for breakfast, lunch, and sometimes snacks and supper. When school is out, food insecurity rises. Beyond safety and supervision, summer programs keep kids mentally engaged, staving off the well-researched “summer slide.” If Maryland wants to meet its ambitious goals for literacy and math proficiency, we ignore summer at our own peril.
The need is urgent, and the gap is wide. According to the Afterschool Alliance’s America After 3 PM Summer Report, 218,095 Maryland children — two in five — whose parents want to enroll them in a summer program are missing out because programs are either unavailable or too expensive.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




When COVID-19 recovery funding for public schools ended, we saw a steep decline in school-based summer programming. We also saw districts shift to half-day models to offset costs, sacrificing convenience for working families. That trend continues this summer.
The stakes are especially high for older youth. Gov. Wes Moore has called on the Department of Juvenile Services to develop a youth summer safety strategy, but that challenge grows steeper as safe gathering spaces for teens continue to shrink. This year’s outlook for summer youth employment is the worst in decades.
When young people gather and incidents occur, media coverage tends to spark hand-wringing about public safety without a corresponding push to expand opportunities for this age group. We can do better.
That’s why the Maryland Out-of-School Time Network has convened a group of leaders to take action through the Maryland Summer Learning and Achievement Task Force. MD-SALT will undertake a yearlong examination of summer programs across the state and make concrete recommendations to Maryland policymakers on expanding access to these critical supports.
Recommendations are already emerging. We need better data to understand where the gaps are most acute. We need expanded public and private investment to increase the number of affordable summer seats statewide. And we need stronger partnerships between communities and schools to offer a wide variety of engaging, age-appropriate programs for students from pre-K through 12th grade.
There is good news in the Afterschool Alliance report: Investing public dollars in summer learning is broadly supported across political affiliations. Families who can access summer experiences for their children overwhelmingly give them high marks. We celebrated National Summer Learning Week July 6-10 to highlight innovative and high-quality programs around the state.
The path forward requires public will at the local and state levels, alongside private and philanthropic investment. One opportunity is to direct future Social Media Lawsuit settlements into resources for high-quality In-Real-Life experiences that give kids a break from screens and build social-emotional capital.
Maryland’s children deserve a summer that is not just a break from school but a bridge to something better. With increased focus, commitment, and resolve, we can make that happen.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: New ICE detention center poses critical test for Colorado
description: If federal immigration authorities are allowed to open a second detention center in Colorado, it will represent a political and moral failure of state leaders and residents. ICE operates one detention center in Colorado, an Aurora site of reported inhumane conditions where many immigrants caught up in the Trump administration’s lawless mass deportation effor[...]
text:
Demonstrators in September gather outside a dormant correctional facility in Hudson that the Trump administration plans to turn into Colorado's newest immigrant detention facility. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)If federal immigration authorities are allowed to open a second detention center in Colorado, it will represent a political and moral failure of state leaders and residents.
ICE operates one detention center in Colorado, an Aurora site of reported inhumane conditions where many immigrants caught up in the Trump administration’s lawless mass deportation efforts are locked away. Now ICE plans to open another northwest of Denver in rural Hudson, where detainees would be subject to the same cruel conditions but even more isolated from legal resources, advocates and public scrutiny.
What goes on at ICE detention centers is abominable. ICE is the out-of-control, homicidal expression of the fascist essence of Trumpism, and its detention centers are the Bastilles of MAGA America. As with the World War II-era incarceration camps for Japanese Americans, the country one day will feel deep shame that ICE’s network of lockups was ever allowed to exist. Coloradans will regret inaction someday if they don’t address this ethical blight by blocking its expansion.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Reports of inhumane conditions at the detention center in Aurora long predate the second Trump administration, but they have become more urgent since the administration began to pursue what President Donald Trump called the “largest domestic deportation operation in American history.”
Earlier this year, immigrant advocates reported ICE’s food offerings in Aurora left detainees underfed and malnourished. This week, Adams County health officials said detention center operators stonewalled their investigation into an inmate’s confirmed case of tuberculosis, apparently in violation of state law, and are unsure if more cases exist. ICE authorities since last year have assiduously avoided accountability, such as with their repeated attempts to block lawful unannounced inspections by members of Congress.
This echoes conditions at ICE facilities around the country, and there’s no reason to believe they’ll be any different at the proposed Hudson facility.



Coloradans can “attack and stop” the effort to site a new ICE detention center in Colorado. Failure to try is a form of complicity.



Life inside the facilities is rotten, but worse, the purpose they serve is reprehensible. Despite the lie from federal officials that the deportation program targets the “worst of the worst,” it is in fact a racist effort to boot from the country as many nonwhite residents without permanent authorization as possible. About 65% of people arrested by ICE in Colorado last year didn’t even have a criminal record. The Aurora facility, like ICE detention centers everywhere, is for many detainees a way station that precedes transfer to foreign countries or prisons. About 12 Aurora detainees last year were sent to the brutal CECOT prison in El Salvador.
The administration has repeatedly trampled the Constitution to pursue deportations, including by denying detainees basic due process rights. Last month, the Trump Justice Department fired a Colorado immigration judge. No official reason was given, but it’s plain the judge angered top officials when she followed the law and granted bond hearings to eligible immigrants.
How can Coloradans stand for more of this? 
“We have seen a complete failure by the Trump Administration in operating ICE detention centers with any decency, accountability or transparency,” U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado said in a social media post this week about the Hudson facility. He said he will “work towards preventing the opening of this facility.”
This is the critical test: Will Bennet and other Coloradans actually do the work to prevent the opening of the facility, or is the outrage just rhetoric?
They’re not helpless. The administration’s doomed plan to convert empty warehouses into mass detention centers illustrates that public pressure, legal challenges and municipal obstruction can be highly effective means of resistance. Community pressure helped scuttle ICE’s plans to use a Virginia warehouse and a Texas warehouse for detention. Salt Lake City leaders sued the Department of Homeland Security over its plans for a large-scale immigration detention center, which are now on hold. Portland, Oregon, leaders invoked land-use rules to oppose the ICE presence there.
“The warehouses were a quick concept to scale up mass deportation,” John Fabbricatore, who was the ICE field office director in Denver during the first Trump administration, told The New York Times last month. He added that “the left was able to throw up immediate roadblocks,” and the warehouse detention plan “was the easiest point for the Democrats to attack and stop that effort.”
Coloradans — from residents to Hudson town council members to state lawmakers to Gov. Jared Polis to members of the state’s congressional delegation — can “attack and stop” the effort to site a new ICE detention center in Colorado. Failure to try is a form of complicity.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Heat-related deaths spiked in last heat wave, worrying health officials as more heat looms
description: Heat-related deaths jumped to 19 in the first half of the summer, with eight of those coming during the brutal heat wave around the Fourth of July, putting the state on track to record the second-most heat deaths in 15 years, new data shows
text:
A young woman cools down with cold water during the summer heat. (Photo by SimpleImages/Getty Stock Images)Heat-related deaths jumped to 19 in the first half of the summer, with eight of those coming during the brutal heat wave around the Fourth of July, putting the state on track to record the second-most heat deaths in 15 years, new data shows.
The latest numbers from the Maryland Department of Health’s Weather-Related Illness Dashboard come as the state heads into another stretch of unseasonably hot, and unhealthy, weather that has health officials urging people to urging Marylanders to take precautions to ensure they, and the people around them, are staying healthy.
“The best way to treat illness is to prevent it altogether,” said Dr. Cheyenne Falat, assistant medical director of the Adult Emergency Department at the University of Maryland Medical Center in Baltimore. “It is important that everyone learns to recognize the signs, not just in themselves, but in others, and know how to respond appropriately.”
After spiking to close to 500 each in the last report, heat-related emergency room or urgent care visits fell to a more typical 142 last week while calls for emergency medical services for the heat dropped to 107. But the 1,061 ER visits during the “heat season” so far, and the 1,042 EMS calls are both just under two-thirds of the way to the records highs set in each category last year.
The department updates its Weather-Related Illness Data Dashboard each Wednesday to record emergency room visits, deaths and emergency medical service calls linked to high temperatures. The most recent update includes data through July 11.
Despite the high number of emergency room visits during the heat wave earlier this month, the number of deaths did not spike until this week because of a reporting lag, as cases were still being evaluated by the medical examiner, according to a statement from the department.

“These represent cases where the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner determined the cause of death as heat-related,” the department’s statement read. “There may be cases that are still pending.”
Dr. Neil Roy, a chief medical officer at Adventist HealthCare Shady Grove Medical Center, and Falat both said they noticed an uptick in patients in their emergency rooms, especially during the heat wave. However, they said this is typical as temperatures rise each summer.
Roy recommends that when people start feeling lightheaded, dizzy or like they’re going to faint, they should first “get away from the heat” and rehydrate before making the decision to come to the hospital.
“But, if you’re not feeling back to normal, I would come to the hospital,” he said. “So if you’re feeling persistently dizzy, you’re feeling like you’re going to pass out, if your loved one is behaving strangely or not behaving appropriately, I would come to the hospital.”
Falat said people who are experiencing signs of neurological abnormalities, like confusion or unresponsiveness, should be taken to the hospital immediately. Patients who show up to emergency rooms with heat stroke are placed in cooling baths to get their body temperatures down quickly, she said.
Both Falat and Roy recommend avoiding the heat as much as possible during very high temperatures and drinking lots of water. They also said to avoid drinking or taking drugs because they can change the body’s ability to respond to heat.
Falat said people who are at extremes of age, like the elderly or young children, may have more difficulty regulating their temperatures, which can make them more susceptible to heat-related illness. She also said those who are physically exerting themselves outside, like athletes, construction workers and emergency responders, can also be at high risks for heat related illness.
Almost three-quarters of heat-related deaths so far this year, 74%, were of people age 65 or older, according to the dashboard. It shows that 41% of people who sought help for heat-related illness were between the ages of 18 and 44, while 29% were older than 65. Another 23% of visits were by people aged 45 to 64, and 7% were below the age of 18.
Despite those statistics, Falat said no one should assume they are not at risk, simply because they are considered to be less susceptible.
“It’s important to know that when temperatures and humidity are this high outside, truly anyone is susceptible,” Falat said. “I don’t want anyone to walk away thinking, ‘I’m not in one of those demographic groups, so I’m OK.’ Anyone is susceptible.”
