name: Nevada Current
title: Boulder City Council seeks to stop data center on BLM land
description: The Boulder City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to appeal the approval of what officials say would be the first data center on U.S. Bureau of Land Management land. The appeal follows a June 26 decision by the Bureau of Land Management to approve the construction of the Townsite Data Center on an 81-acre plot […]
text:
Boulder City Attorney Brittany Walker argued BLM's approval of the data center was a departure from BLM precedent and procedure, giving the city the right to appeal the decision “especially for a brand new use that, to my knowledge, has never been authorized on BLM land.” (BLM photo)The Boulder City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to appeal the approval of what officials say would be the first data center on U.S. Bureau of Land Management land.
The appeal follows a June 26 decision by the Bureau of Land Management to approve the construction of the Townsite Data Center on an 81-acre plot of BLM land in the Eldorado Valley desert about three miles southwest of Boulder City residences.
In addition to the data center, the facility  would include a battery energy storage system, an electrical substation, and biodiesel emergency backup generators.
Townsite Solar 2 LLC  — the project developer — originally received federal approval in 2023 to build a solar power generation and battery storage facility on the parcel, but requested an amended right-of-way grant in 2025 to build a data center instead.
City Councilman Steve Walton expressed disbelief that the federal government accepted a prior environmental impact study for a solar farm to allow construction of a data center.
“I don’t know in any world how they could have made the statement that that project is in any way similar to the original solar energy production and battery energy storage application,” Walton said. “This is absolutely out of line, just ridiculous. I don’t know how they could even come to that conclusion.”
Boulder City Attorney Brittany Walker argued the move was a departure from BLM precedent and procedure, giving the city the right to appeal the decision “especially for a brand new use that, to my knowledge, has never been authorized on BLM land.”
“The BLM essentially, sweepingly, approved a new land use without following processes in federal law, which include a meaningful engagement process with the City of Boulder City,” Walker said. 
Boulder City Council said the BLM did not consult them when making their determination, adding they only found out about the move after the change was approved.
“We’re taking on a giant,” said Mayor Pro Tempore Sherri Jorgensen.
“I cannot believe that this happened, but here we are.”
The approval to build on federal land effectively strips the city of any authority over the project, which was originally moving through the city’s land leasing process. During that process, the city’s planning commission voted unanimously in May not to recommend the construction of the data center on city-owned land.
Townsite Solar 2 LLC withdrew its application to build their data center on city-owned land following BLM approval to build on federal land. 
Trump’s ‘AI Action Plan’
The BLM determined the data center “is essentially like the original” solar energy facility that underwent an environmental assessment in 2023, according to a BLM document. The agency noted both projects are industrial uses that are predominantly electrical in nature and that both would connect to external electrical infrastructure via the same proposed utility corridor. 
The new project on federal land would also use the same location, same acreage, and same perimeter as the originally planned solar facility, according to the BLM.
In the record of decision approving the change, federal land managers said air quality in and around Boulder City would not be impacted by the data center. The agency notes the facility’s biodiesel back-up generators would only be used during testing and system emergencies.
The proposed data center would use a closed-loop cooling system with direct-to-chip liquid cooling, which does not rely on evaporative cooling and uses less water. Still, the data center is expected to use up to 2,000 gallons of water annually. 
It would also require a one-time initial fill of 400,000 gallons of water, and another 500,000 gallons of water during the construction phase as a dust suppressant, according to the BLM.
Federal land managers acknowledged the data center “poses a larger fire risk than solar panel arrays,” but argued the project area and immediate surrounding areas are open desert with minimal vegetative fuel.
Development plans for the data center say the facility will use cooling towers to move heat produced at the site upward several hundred feet above the buildings and away from ground level.
In Townsite Solar 2 LLC’s development plan, the company said the expansion of data centers on federal land is vital to support technologies like artificial intelligence. 
The company said the development of data centers on federal land is also a top priority for the United States government, as outlined in the Trump administration’s “America’s AI Action Plan” which was published by the White House in 2025. 
The plan establishes new categorical exclusions under federal law to cover data center-related actions, including making federal lands available for data center construction by directing agencies large land portfolios to identify sites suited to large-scale development.
Under the plan, the Department of Energy identified four sites “well-situated for large-scale data centers,” including Idaho National Laboratory, Tennessee’s  Oak Ridge Reservation, Kentuky’s Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant, and Georgia’s Savannah River Site. 
If implemented on BLM lands, the plan could have major implications for public lands throughout the West, and especially in Nevada where about 80% of the land is managed by the federal government.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Legal powerhouse John Morgan wades into OpenAI battle over FSU shooting
description: One of the nation’s most powerful law firms is wading into the war against OpenAI, representing two students claiming ChatGPT’s negligence may have caused their wounds in a shooting rampage at Florida State University last spring. John Morgan, a Democrat mega-donor and founder of the new “Common Ground” party in Florida, is the latest Florida […]
text:
John Morgan's law firm represents two FSU students wounded in a mass shooting in their lawsuits against OpenAI, ChatGPT. (Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix).One of the nation’s most powerful law firms is wading into the war against OpenAI, representing two students claiming ChatGPT’s negligence may have caused their wounds in a shooting rampage at Florida State University last spring.
John Morgan, a Democrat mega-donor and founder of the new “Common Ground” party in Florida, is the latest Florida legal figure to recognize that as the burgeoning artificial intelligence industry swells, so do its alleged shortcomings. Most recently, this is reflected in the legal onslaught against ChatGPT for instructing alleged shooter Phoenix Ikner how to use his guns — mere minutes before he killed two and injured five others.
“OpenAI’s alleged negligence in these cases is the latest example of a company valuing growth and profits over public safety,” Morgan and attorney Christian Leger said in a joint statement. “Our clients, two young students who have had their lives disrupted and their sense of safety shattered, hope their lawsuit compels OpenAI to do better and protect people from the dangers of their products going forward.”
Morgan & Morgan’s clients are Elizabeth Mall and Madison Askins, two students harmed during the attack. Although Mall’s injuries haven’t been disclosed, Askins was interviewed from her Tallahassee Memorial Hospital bed days after the shooting, when she described being shot in the hip and playing dead.
Both suits seek a jury trial and demand punitive damages, although the figure isn’t enumerated.
The suits, nearly identical and filed in Tallahassee’s federal court on Monday, add to two other cases and one planned suit against OpenAI for its role in the April 17, 2025, attack. The family of South Carolina man Tiru Chabba, one of two men killed in the shooting, sued in federal court while student Alianna Grant, shot three times, filed in state court.
The widow of the other murdered man, Robert Morales, also plans to sue the company. But the biggest legal headlines have been drawn by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who launched both a civil suit and a first-in-the-nation criminal investigation into OpenAI to examine whether executives or developers could be found criminally liable for the murders.
“If ChatGPT were a person, it would be facing charges for murder,” Uthmeier said at the time. Both Askins’ and Mall’s complaints begin with his quote.
What’s in the suits?
Both suits seek damages for medical expenses, pain and suffering, mental anguish, and emotional distress, alleging Mall and Askins were, “as a direct and proximate result” of OpenAI, harmed by the company’s “aiding and abetting behavior.”
They allege that Ikner would have been “wholly incapable” of properly identifying, loading, and using his guns if it weren’t for ChatGPT — which they say “actively assisted and encouraged” the mass shooting.
“Ikner’s attack was carefully planned with the sycophantic assistance of his favorite chatbot — ChatGPT,” the complaint says.
“ChatGPT had information indicating that Ikner was an FSU student, had been bullied, struggled socially, had mental-health issues, was interested in extremist ideology, had discussed terrorism and mass shootings, had uploaded guns, and had asked about weapons, ammunition, lethality, notoriety, and crowd timing.
“ChatGPT failed to connect the dots, failed to escalate the situation for human review, ChatGPT failed to suspend or restrict Ikner’s access, and failed to trigger any effective intervention,” the brief continues.
They referred to thousands of messages between 20-year-old Ikner and ChatGPT in the year leading to the attack. The Phoenix previously reported that conversations included graphic sexual descriptions of a minor and another college student, sexual conversations about family members, and repeated references to Timothy McVeigh, the Oklahoma City bomber.
He consulted the chatbot about weapons, how Florida treats school shooters, and the busiest time at the student union. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.
Just three minutes before Ikner opened fire, he asked ChatGPT how to remove the safety on his shotgun. It told him.
In an earlier statement to the Phoenix, OpenAI denied all wrongdoing and insisted it has been cooperating with authorities.
Morgan, 70, continually ranks in the Top 10 of Orlando’s most powerful people. He employs people in all 50 states and is worth roughly $1.5 billion, according to Forbes. Morgan & Morgan is worth $2 billion.
In Florida, Morgan is a frequent donor to Democratic candidates. He was architect of ballot initiatives that raised the state’s minimum wage and legalized marijuana.
Last year, he toyed with running for governor — initially as an independent. Morgan later said that, while he wouldn’t enter the race, he was starting a new “middle ground” party called Common Ground. He said it’s designed for Floridians who feel “left behind” by Democrats and Republicans.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC’s largest cities poised to strengthen curfews amid growing ‘teen takeovers’
description: “If we don’t get a handle on this, the consequences may become fatal.” Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Chief Estella Patterson told the city council’s safety committee Tuesday that “teen takeovers” have become a growing problem nationwide. It works like this: A post appears on social media inviting youth to gather at a designated spot. Hundreds, in some […]
text:
Charlotte Mecklenburg Police Department steps up enforcement amid a rise in 'teen takeovers' in July.  (Photo: Charlotte Mecklenburg Police Department)“If we don’t get a handle on this, the consequences may become fatal.”
Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Chief Estella Patterson told the city council’s safety committee Tuesday that “teen takeovers” have become a growing problem nationwide.
It works like this: A post appears on social media inviting youth to gather at a designated spot. Hundreds, in some cases thousands, of teenagers turn out late at night, sometimes overwhelming a neighborhood.
Large swarms of teens have gathered in communities across North and South Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, and Georgia this summer. Some gatherings have resulted in fights and shootings, like an event on the Fourth of July weekend in Raleigh that attracted 8,000 unsupervised juveniles to Brier Creek and Glenwood South.
Deputy Chief Jackie Bryley (L) and Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Chief Estella Patterson (R) discuss the difficulty in managing hundreds of unsupervised juveniles this summer. (Photo: City of Charlotte)
More than 200 teens also gathered at a park in Charlotte on the holiday weekend. Patterson said the only reason that takeover didn’t get out of hand was because the city had over 200 officers patrolling the region.
“It is not sustainable to deploy that many officers every single day. We don’t have the staff, we have the budget for it,” said Patterson.
“What we’re experiencing is large numbers of our youth gathering, and they’re meeting up to cause fights, disturbances, and just overall disorder,” echoed Deputy Chief Jackie Bryley.
Bryley said while officers have stepped up curfew enforcement, many teens don’t carry identification and may not be willing to share their real name, age or home address.
Since January, Charlotte has recorded more than 1,532 criminal incidents with at least one juvenile suspect. Nearly one-third of those criminal incidents involving juveniles occurred between 8:00 p.m. and 5:59 a.m.
This week, the council’s safety committee endorsed the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department’s proposal to modify the city’s ordinance to a stricter 9 p.m. curfew for all children under the age of 18 every night of the week. The current youth protection curfew is tiered based on age.
Exceptions would stay in place for a teen who is accompanied by a parent or guardian or traveling to or from a place of employment. Attending or traveling to a recreational or sporting event that is supervised by adults or sponsored by the city or civic organization would still be permitted.
“Can we hope for a significant change from changing the curfew if there is a disregard for law enforcement?” asked Councilman Ed Driggs.
Patterson said Charlotte law enforcement will take a progressive approach starting with education or a warning before escalating to enforcement action.
“We recognize that many of our youth want to do the right thing, but then happen to be in the wrong place at the wrong time and things go badly,” said Patterson.
The Charlotte City Council is expected to take formal action on the stricter curfew when it meets in August. The Queen City is also promoting a teen summer jam series with the hope that the structured events will give youth a safe gathering spot on weekends.
The city of Raleigh is also weighing an 11 p.m. citywide curfew for people under 18. Raleigh’s City Council is scheduled to vote on that and possible fines for violators at its August 18 session.
Unsecured firearms increase the risk
Rep. Marcia Morey (D-Durham) told NC Newsline this week that when she was a district court judge, she proposed a curfew following a rash of carjackings and burglaries by young people.
That proposal didn’t go anywhere, so she’s pleased to see cities working on more proactive solutions this summer.
Rep. Marcia Morey (Photo: NC General Assembly)
“Kids have no business being on the street after 11:00 p.m. or midnight, unless they’re working. There can be exceptions,” said Morey.
Morey said increased access to guns has made the problem worse. During the teen takeover in Raleigh July 4th, police arrested 29 people and confiscated 11 firearms. A week later, a July 11th takeover in Charlotte attracted 300 juveniles. Three were arrested for carrying a concealed weapon and possession of a firearm by a minor.
Morey said parents must play a bigger role in the solution — including knowing where their children are each night, and locking up any firearms they may own.
“If you have a gun, [if] it’s in a car or a truck and you leave, lock it up,” said Morey.
Morey introduced legislation in the 2025 session to make it unlawful to leave a firearm in an unattended motor vehicle unless the vehicle was locked and the firearm secured with a trigger lock or stored in a lock box. Republican leadership did not give her bill a hearing.
Billy Lassiter, deputy secretary with the Division of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention, is also appealing to parents to secure their guns.
Lassiter asked state lawmakers to provide $2.26 million in recurring funds for the NC Secure All Firearms Effectively campaign, which provides gun locks and safe storage messaging for firearm owners.
Two NC children die from firearms each week. State agency wants consistent funding to combat that.

While $1 million in funding was included in Gov. Josh Stein’s recommended budget, state lawmakers did not fund the program in the final 2026 Appropriations Act.
More than 100,000 guns have been stolen in North Carolina over the past decade, often ending up in the hands of children or criminals, according to Lassiter.
“We need some movement in gun safety because guns outnumber people now,” said Morey. “To me, that’s the most common sense, low-hanging fruit we could do.”

name: WyoFile
title: Feds push state management for threatened grizzly bear
authors: by Hanna Merzbach and Nicky Ouellet, Wyoming Public Radio
description:
Change in management doesn’t affect endangered listing status or allow hunting seasons, but critics argue there’s still much work to be done for species’ survival.
The post Feds push state management for threatened grizzly bear appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is preparing to return management of the threatened grizzly bear to the states.
The announcement came from the secretary of the interior and governors of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming via a windy livestream from Big Sky, Montana, on Tuesday afternoon.
“The endangered species list is not a dean’s list,” Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon said. “It’s time that this bear graduates.”
Gordon, Idaho Gov. Brad Little and Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte have long pushed for removing the bear from the Endangered Species Act list, which includes both threatened and endangered species. The proposal would keep the bears on that list but have states — not the federal government — manage them, said Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.
“ We’re moving responsibility back to the states, not delisting, but moving responsibility back to the states because of the great recovery,” Burgum said.
From left, Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks Director Christy Clark, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik, Idaho Gov. Brad Little, Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon announce plans to return grizzly bear management to the states July 14, 2026, in Big Sky, Mont. (Nick Mott)
“The revised proposal supports the Trump administration’s goal of reducing unnecessary regulatory complexity, empowering states and tribes and ensuring wildlife management decisions are practical, science-based and effective on the ground,” according to a press release from the U.S. Department of the Interior. “The rule does not change the grizzly bear’s listing status under the Endangered Species Act and does not affect existing experimental population designations.”
The Fish and Wildlife Service is reopening a 30-day public comment period on the revised proposed 4(d) rule. The revision updates a January 2025 proposal and focuses solely on the 4(d) provisions. The service is not proposing changes to, and is not seeking additional comment on, other components of the January 2025 proposed rule.
The governors said under the 4(d) rule, states would not have the authority to have hunting seasons.
This announcement applies to the about 2,000 bears in Wyoming, Idaho, Montana and Washington — about half of which are in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem.
The last time the Fish and Wildlife Service tried to delist grizzlies in 2017, Wyoming and Idaho created hunting seasons. Wyoming issued 22 tags, but the hunt never came to fruition, as environmentalists sued to resume protections and a judge ruled in their favor.
Kristen Draney and Doug McWhirter with Wyoming Game and Fish Department take notes during a small group discussion on grizzly bear management Nov. 15, 2017, at The Virginian Lodge in Jackson. The groups discussed monitoring, research, conflict, outreach and education, and grizzly bear hunting. (Ryan Dorgan)
Wyoming, Idaho and Montana have argued it’s time for federal protections to go away. They say grizzly numbers are up and they’ve met population targets.
“ As you heard here, the goal of the Endangered Species Act is recovery,” said Gianforte. “Today, that recovery is being recognized. Recovery was never the end of the story, though, for this iconic species. The next chapter is about stewardship. State management does not mean the work is over. In many ways, it means the work becomes even more important.”
“It’s just more than fitting and proper that the state wildlife management agencies and all three of our states work together on a lot of cross-boundary wildlife issues, whether it’s management, whether it’s ungulate populations, fill in the blank,” added Little. “This is the right thing to do for this part of the country, and it’s the right thing to do for the United States of America, so I couldn’t be happier to be here.”





Click to enlarge: Map showing historical and current grizzly bear range in North America.  (Lisa Landenburger/USGS – IGBST)

But many environmentalists say the bears occupy only a slice of their historic range, populations aren’t genetically diverse enough and states aren’t ready to take on management.
“This is a decision being made for political reasons, it is not based on science, in the best interest of the survival of the species, or in compliance with the requirements of the Endangered Species Act,” said Greg LeDonne, Idaho director of Western Watersheds Project. “It’s clearly too soon to remove federal protections in light of the continued lack of connectivity, ongoing habitat destruction and modification due to climate change, and record numbers of grizzly bear mortalities in 2025 even under existing protections.”
Western Watersheds issued a press release that framed the proposal as a step toward delisting, which has yet to be confirmed. The group also pointed to a recent federal court ruling that says recovery of an ESA species must occur throughout that species’ historic range, not just where they’re currently found, which could expand the area where grizzly bear recovery should be expected.
How we got here
Grizzlies have largely been on the Endangered Species Act list since 1975.
The last proposal from the Fish and Wildlife Service, released in the final days of the Biden administration, would have kept them on the list with some tweaks, such as giving landowners more flexibility around killing bears that threaten livestock.
After receiving more than 200,000 comments, the Fish and Wildlife Service was supposed to finalize the grizzly regulations by Jan. 31, as mandated by a court in Idaho. But the agency asked for an extension, citing staff turnover and regulatory backlog.
Federal District Judge David C. Nye approved the extension request until Dec. 18, highlighting that the final rule must comply with the ESA and either revise or remove the entire listing for grizzly bears in the lower 48 states.
Environmental groups expect the Fish and Wildlife Service to release its new proposal in the Federal Register any day.
Hanna Merzbach is the Wyoming Public Media-based Mountain West News Bureau reporter. The bureau is a collaboration of public radio newsrooms in seven Western states and NPR.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: AG Bird: ‘There is no acceptable amount’ of Medicaid fraud in Iowa
description: Members of Iowa’s newly created Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force met Wednesday for their inaugural meeting to begin crafting recommendations to stop incidents of fraud in the taxpayer supported healthcare program. The 11-person task force, led by Attorney General Brenna Bird, established five working groups that Bird said will be the “engine” that drive[...]
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, center, led Iowa's first Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force meeting July 15, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Members of Iowa’s newly created Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force met Wednesday for their inaugural meeting to begin crafting recommendations to stop incidents of fraud in the taxpayer supported healthcare program.
The 11-person task force, led by Attorney General Brenna Bird, established five working groups that Bird said will be the “engine” that drives the research, analyses and problem-solving recommendations the task force will include in a final report due to the governor by Oct. 29.
“We’re here to focus our collective resources and expertise on a single vital goal, and that’s to eliminate Medicaid fraud, waste, and abuse in Iowa,” Bird said to members of the task force.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Kim Reynolds signed an executive order July 1 creating the task force with a mission of “eradicating” Medicaid fraud.
Iowa’s task force aligns with federal efforts to curb Medicaid fraud, including the fraud task force led by Vice President J.D. Vance and a provision in the Republican-backed reconciliation bill, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill” act, that will require states to pay for Medicaid payments made in error if their average error rate is above a certain threshold. 
In the most recent report for Iowa, the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reported the state had a projected improper payment rate of 1.9%. 
Bird, when asked if Medicaid fraud was an issue in Iowa, said “there is no acceptable amount of Medicaid fraud” and that providers committing fraud need to be held accountable in criminal and civil courts. 
“When providers are committing that Medicaid fraud, it is taking money away from the taxpayers that was supposed to be used to help people that really need the Medicaid program and depend on it,” Bird said. “So it’s important that our Medicaid program has integrity.” 
Bird said the task force pulls key partners together in the state to stop fraud from happening in the first place and to develop a system for investigations, prosecution and the civil recovery of erroneous payments. 
In addition to Bird, the 11-person task force includes: 

Larry Johnson, principal deputy director at Iowa Health and Human Services
Jennifer Vermeer, plan president for Molina Healthcare of Iowa, one of the state’s three Medicaid managed-care providers
Kraig Paulsen, director of the Iowa Department of Management and director of Iowa HHS
Aaron Baack, director of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing
Dax Oberreuter, from the Office of the Governor 
Stephan Bayens, commissioner at the Iowa Department of Public Safety
Colleen Askvig, a representative from Iowa Total Care, another contracted Medicaid managed-care provider 
Jeremy Ingrim, director Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit
Lee Grossman, the director of Iowa Medicaid 
Teresa Hursey, president of Wellpoint Iowa, formerly Amerigroup Iowa, the third Medicaid managed-care provider in the state

Dean Lerner, a former director of DIAL and a former Iowa assistant attorney general, said the task force is “a bunch of political self-aggrandizement” considering the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit already exists with a set mission of investigating and prosecuting providers making fraudulent Medicaid claims.
He said if the state wants to crack down on Medicaid fraud, it should instead offer additional support to the control unit, especially as there is evidence that Iowa consistently funds its Medicaid Fraud Control Unit at significantly lower rates than states with comparable Medicaid spending. 
“It is nonsensical to create a task force to do what the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit is already by law required to do,” Lerner said. 
As its first order of business, the task force approved five work groups whose reports will help inform the task force’s final report to the governor. 
Each working group was assigned a different focus, like optimizing federal alignment, investing in technology and data analytics, establishing integrity quality initiatives for high-risk services, supporting Managed Care Organizations and enhancing fraud awareness in the state and public reporting of suspected fraud. 
The task force meetings will be streamed to the public and Iowans can submit recommendations to the task force at MedicaidTaskForceComments@ag.iowa.gov
“There’s a lot of work ahead of us,” Bird said to task members. “It’s a pretty complex issue, as you know, but there’s a great deal of good that can come from bringing a group of talented people like you together to work on such an important issue for Iowans.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Ramsey County sues DHS over failure to hand over evidence in potential kidnapping of U.S. citizen
description: Ramsey County officials are suing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, seeking evidence related to potential crimes committed by federal agents against a St. Paul man during Operation Metro Surge, including kidnapping, false imprisonment and burglary.  On Jan. 18, immigration agents forcibly entered the home of ChongLy “Scott” Thao, a U.S. citizen, with[...]
text:
ChongLy Scott Thao, a U.S. citizen, was detained after ICE agents and other law enforcement officers conducted an immigration raid at his home in St. Paul Jan. 18, 2026. (Photo by Leah Millis/Reuters) (This photo is not for republication.)Ramsey County officials are suing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, seeking evidence related to potential crimes committed by federal agents against a St. Paul man during Operation Metro Surge, including kidnapping, false imprisonment and burglary. 
On Jan. 18, immigration agents forcibly entered the home of ChongLy “Scott” Thao, a U.S. citizen, without a warrant, according to the lawsuit. The agents handcuffed Thao, removed him from his home in just Crocs and boxers, and questioned him in the car for about an hour before returning him to his house. A Reuters photo of agents removing Thao became an iconic symbol of the brutal tactics used by immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge, which DHS has described as the largest immigration enforcement action in its history.
On April 13, Ramsey County Attorney John Choi announced his office sent a letter — called a Touhy demand — to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, formally requesting information relating to the case. 
In May, the federal government requested extra time to respond to the county’s request for information, Choi said, but has since gone silent.
“Our hope … is to compel the cooperation and the sharing of information, so that we in Ramsey County can do, very simply, an investigation,” Choi said during a press conference Wednesday announcing the lawsuit. “To get to the truth, to evaluate whether or not Minnesota law has been broken, and to uphold the rule of law wherever the facts take us and what the law prescribes, and to do that without fear or favor.”
The Ramsey County officials are seeking the identities of the federal agents who entered Thao’s home and forcibly removed him. The agents wore masks and swapped out their license plates, obscuring their identities from both the public and local investigators, according to the lawsuit. 
In the complaint, Ramsey County officials pointed to several recent examples of cooperation between federal and local law enforcement agencies: the investigation into attacks on Minnesota lawmakers last summer; the response to the Annunciation school shooting; and prosecutions of gang members. 
“This shift from historical practices of cooperation is reflected in Surge related cases in Hennepin County, where federal officials initially agreed to cooperate, but then withdrew cooperation, even blocked crime scene access,” the lawsuit reads. 
(After months of stonewalling, drawing a similar lawsuit from the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office in March, federal authorities this week handed over evidence related to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and the shooting of Venezuelan national Julio Sosa-Celis.)
The lawsuit requests that a federal judge order the federal government to cooperate with local authorities, fulfill their requests for evidence and cover the county’s legal fees.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Omaha joins Lincoln in restoring $15 minimum wage for all workers
description: The Omaha City Council on Tuesday followed its counterpart in Lincoln and passed a local ordinance keeping its minimum wage at $15 an hour for all workers.
text:
Omaha City Council members Pete Festersen (left) and Aimee Melton (right), listen to public testimony at a previous hearing. (Photo by Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)The Omaha City Council on Tuesday followed its counterpart in Lincoln and passed a local ordinance keeping its minimum wage at $15 an hour for all workers.
The council voted 4-3 to approve the ordinance after rejecting a proposal to put it on file, which would have essentially delayed a decision until a later date, giving Omaha a chance to see what happens in the state’s case against Lincoln.
In Nebraska, a possible new dynamic emerges as blue cities push back against a red state government

Councilwoman Aimee Melton said she doesn’t believe Omaha has the power or the authority to pass a law that is in conflict with the state law, and she said putting the proposed ordinance on file would allow a vote later if a court rules in favor of Lincoln.
“We should allow the process to work and see what happens in Lincoln,” Melton said.
Lincoln passed an ordinance on May 11 keeping its minimum wage at $15 an hour for all workers, including youth workers, as well as tying future increases to the Consumer Price Index.
That’s the way the law was written when Nebraska voters passed it in 2022, but the Legislature changed it earlier this year, setting a lower minimum wage of $13.50 for people under 16 and also limiting future increases to no more than 1.75%.
Nebraska AG sues city of Lincoln over minimum wage rule at odds with state law

Attorney General Mike Hilgers last month filed a lawsuit seeking an injunction to stop the Lincoln law from taking effect. A judge has yet to rule on that request.
Council President Danny Begley said he believes the city should respect the widespread support from Omaha voters, who elected overwhelmingly in 2022 to support raising the minimum wage to $15 for all workers.
“I heard you — what you said,” Begley said. “Seventy-eight percent of my district. Seventy point two percent in Omaha. All seven districts said yes.”
Begley was joined in approving the ordinance by council members Pete Festersen, LaVonya Goodwin and Ron Hug. Melton, Don Rowe and Brinker Harding voted no.
“We serve at the pleasure of the state, and for us to pass this, puts us in direct violation of state law, in my opinion,” Rowe said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Forward Party sues Secretary of State over disqualifying candidates from November ballot
description: New Mexico’s nascent minor political party sued Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver on Tuesday and alleged that her office has enforced “severe and unequal” barriers for its candidates to make the Nov. 3 general election ballot.
text:
New Mexico Forward Party Chair Bob Perls, left, is pictured with former New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman on April 15, 2025. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico’s nascent minor political party sued Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver on Tuesday and alleged that her office has enforced “severe and unequal” barriers for its candidates to make the Nov. 3 general election ballot.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Forward Party filed the lawsuit, which claims its candidates’ First and Fourteenth Amendment rights have been violated, in U.S. District Court. Like another ballot access case recently filed by independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Miyagishima, party officials allege that they have to gather excessive numbers of signatures compared to candidates running with either of the major political parties.
Since the party only gained official minor party status earlier this year and still has a small registered voter base, its candidates were required to gather more than 14,000 signatures for statewide offices, the lawsuit alleges. By contrast, Democratic and Republican candidates seeking statewide office must gather approximately 2,500 and 2,350, respectively. 
New Mexico Forward Party Chair Bob Perls in a news release said he had previously spent a decade working to address “discriminatory and unfair ballot access laws” in the Legislature when he was president of New Mexico Open Elections. He noted that he plans to work with state lawmakers, regardless of party affiliation, in the 2027 legislative session to reduce and equalize signature-gathering requirements.
Perls, who unsuccessfully filed to run for U.S. Senate against incumbent Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), told Source NM that he and the state Forward Party’s candidates intentionally targeted races that would otherwise go uncontested.
“We do not have crowded ballots. In fact, we have the emptiest ballots in the nation,” Perls said. “All we’re trying to do is give people choices.”
He said the signature requirements make it “impossible” for anyone who isn’t a Democrat or Republican to get on the ballot.
His party’s lawsuit asks a judge to put several of the disqualified Forward Party candidates on the ballot.
A spokesperson for the New Mexico Secretary of State on Wednesday said the office had not yet received a copy of the lawsuit.
Perls’ party in June filed signatures to place five candidates on the November ballot: Perls for U.S. Senate; former Albuquerque Public Schools Chief Financial Officer Michael Vigil for Office of the State Auditor; and candidates for the Public Education Commission and county magistrate judgeships.
Former Democratic presidential candidate Andrew Yang visited Santa Fe in April to announce that the Forward Party would seek minor party status. Tenets for the party, which has fielded candidates across the nation regardless of whether they were previously Democrats or Republicans, include treating “everyone with dignity and respect” and acting “with ethics, integrity and compassion.” The New Mexico Forward Party gained that status with the state in May.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi teachers say new state-mandated process for buying classroom supplies is ‘insane, cumbersome, frustrating’
description: A classroom at a Hattiesburg child care center displays educational materials, alphabet chartsand a February calendar. Providers say extending hours would require additional staffing and overnight accommodations
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Weeks before the first day of school, teachers across Mississippi say state leaders have made it more difficult for them to access money for classroom supplies. 
Educators have to complete training before they’re able to spend the money the state gives them for classroom supplies, but teachers say the live training has been hard to access — the online meetings have been filled to capacity. Teachers also say that to buy from local vendors, they now have to go through an arduous reimbursement process. 
The money for teachers’ classroom supplies comes from the Education Enhancement Fund, or procurement card program. EEF, established in 2012, gives every K-12 public school teacher $748 — around $25 million in total — to buy supplies for their classrooms. But educators have long said they get the money too late for it to be useful. A report released last year by State Auditor Shad White’s office found that a bulk of the money is locked for teachers as they prepare their classrooms because of the state-mandated Aug. 1 deadline to activate the cards.
Teachers shop for classroom supplies in a repurposed school bus operated by Old School Tutoring and Toys.  Credit: David Bates
This year, Mississippi Department of Education leaders said they wanted to make the process easier for teachers by giving districts access to the money on July 15 and switching from physical cards to a digital wallet platform.
The agency has a one-year $573,000 contract with the platform ClassWallet, according to Shanderia Minor, a spokesperson for the state Education Department. 
The new platform is used in several states and allows teachers to purchase supplies directly from online, pre-approved vendors. State Superintendent Lance Evans said ClassWallet streamlines the process of buying classroom supplies, and the change reflects input from school district leaders across Mississippi. 
One frustration for teachers is that many of the vendors they buy supplies from are not included in the list of more than 160 vendors on ClassWallet’s marketplace, where teachers can spend their EEF money.
According to the state Education Department’s website, five Mississippi-based vendors are approved for teacher reimbursements, as are Walmart and TeachersPayTeachers, an online marketplace for classroom supplies. 
But teachers then have to spend their own money upfront. Additionally, their purchase must be approved before they can be reimbursed. 
If teachers want to buy from local vendors not included on that list, the state Department of Education must first contact that vendor to ensure they’ll give teachers itemized receipts and that the items will be tax exempt. Then the vendor will be added to the list, and teachers can submit reimbursement requests through ClassWallet.
Because of the administrative burden, educators are concerned they’ll have to wait weeks to get their money back.
“The words I’ve heard are ‘insane,’ ‘cumbersome,’ and ‘frustrating,’” said Kelly Riley, executive director of Mississippi Professional Educators. Riley said she’s received numerous emails from educators across the state who are confused by the new process and annoyed by the extra layers of bureaucracy. “There’s just a lot of unknowns at this point.”
White’s office released a statement on social media Tuesday that the education agency has “misinformed the public” about the program and called on the state Education Department to rectify issues with the new process. 
“Teachers will again, through no fault of their own, have to spend their own funds to get classroom supplies while they’re forced to navigate through bureaucratic hoops to get the money promised to them,” the statement reads. “This should not be complicated.”
State Education Department officials say they’ve been communicating with districts for months, but some teachers say the change has caught them by surprise. Additionally, educators must first attend or watch one of five virtual training sessions scheduled this month before their district can activate their accounts. 
David Bates, a former teacher, now runs a tutoring service and classroom supply store for educators in Pascagoula, Miss. Bates drives a school bus packed with supplies to local schools for teachers to purchase what they need with their EEF funds.  Credit: David Bates
Many teachers say they were unable to access the first training on July 13. 
Marie Lane, a longtime special education teacher in north Mississippi, was one of those teachers waiting for the Zoom meeting to start on Monday. 
“At 8:40 a.m., I had my notebook out, my laptop plugging in, all excited,” she said. But as the 9 a.m. meeting started, Lane was still waiting to get in. She got a message a few minutes later that the webinar had reached capacity. 
Lane hopes she can get into one of the other meetings. She’s been gleaning what she can from other educators on social media. That’s how Lane realized how much the state was paying ClassWallet to administer the EEF program. 
“That really grates on my last nerve,” she said. “That’s money that could be spent in the classrooms for these kids.”
She’s doubtful she’ll get what she needs for her class — such as cups for paint to make learning more accessible for her students, a walkie-talkie to communicate with her assistant teacher, dim lamps for her students with sensory needs — before the first day of school on Aug. 3.
“There’s no way at this point I’ll be able to submit a list and get it by the time students are back,” she said. “Lots of times when you’re teaching and someone isn’t getting what we’re doing, you think, ‘If I could run to Walmart real quick for Play-Doh or beads, I could help them.’ But now, if we don’t want to spend our own money, we’re going to have to place an order, wait for it to be accepted and delivered.”
Lane plans to use the money she’s gotten from a recent yard sale and selling items on Facebook to buy the supplies she needs. 
“We as teachers have enough on our plate,” she said. “For special education teachers like me, it’s still required that our students meet certain standards. Meeting those without the supplies we need is going to be really tough.”
Riley said that’s a frustration being voiced by educators across the state. They’re also concerned about the platform’s vendor list, she said, which includes about 50 homeschool-centric vendors.
ClassWallet’s website promotes the new federal tax scholarship program and includes testimonials from homeschoolers and education savings account recipients across the country. 
Jean Cook, a spokesperson for the state education agency, said the homeschool vendors are included on ClassWallet’s list because the platform operates across the country. The Mississippi-specific vendor list will be updated weekly, according to the agency’s website. 
Keyana Hawthorne is an 11th-grade teacher at Murrah High School in Jackson, Mississippi.  Credit: Keyana Hawthorne
A statement released by the education agency on Monday notes, “Many other states do not have programs like Mississippi’s that give teachers money to buy supplemental instructional materials for their individual classrooms.”
David Bates, a former teacher, is the owner of one of the Mississippi-approved vendors — Old School Learning Depot in Pascagoula. His business provides tutoring services for students after school and sells classroom supplies for teachers. In past years, Bates drove a bus packed with supplies to local schools, allowing teachers to buy in-person with their EEF cards without leaving school property. 
But now, he estimates that the new process will result in a $60,000 loss in revenue for his business because teachers will want to avoid spending their own money.
“For a mom-and-pop shop, that is a pretty big chunk of money,” he said. 
“I’m not combating change,” Bates said. “I just want the opportunity to be part of the change. I’m frustrated about last-minute rollout and last-minute communication about how to make this work for everyone.”
Keyana Hawthorne, an English teacher at Murrah High School in Jackson, was initially skeptical about the agency switching to ClassWallet. Now, she said she hates that she was right. 
Hawthorne plans to attend a training on July 28, which she said conflicts with the professional development she receives in the days leading up to school. Her students return July 29. 
As a result, all of her classroom supplies will come out of her own pocket this year, Hawthorne said. She’s planning to buy them in increments because she can’t afford to buy everything in one go. With two children of her own to buy school supplies for, Hawthorne said she’s overwhelmed, frustrated and disappointed. 
“This is pulling from my little budget, and it makes me question: How are we supposed to survive over here?” she said. “I’m so frustrated right now. This is what happens when teachers aren’t asked to sit at the tables where crucial decisions are being made.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Elissa Slotkin endorses Matt Maasdam in Democratic primary for her former House seat
description: U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) is putting her political capital behind Matt Maasdam as he seeks the Democratic Party nomination for the 7th Congressional District in the Aug. 4 primary. The district was represented by Slotkin before she ran for the U.S. Senate in 2024. It is currently occupied by U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin speaks at the Detroit NAACP Fight For Freedom Fund Dinner in Detroit, Mich., on April 26, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) is putting her political capital behind Matt Maasdam as he seeks the Democratic Party nomination for the 7th Congressional District in the Aug. 4 primary.
The district was represented by Slotkin before she ran for the U.S. Senate in 2024. It is currently occupied by U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), who won the seat after Slotkin ran for the Senate seat vacated by the retirement of former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D-Lansing).
“Mid-Michigan is where it all began for me, representing this district — from Charlotte, to Lansing, to Owosso, to Brighton, to South Lyon — in the U.S. House for six years,” Slotkin said in a statement. “Matt has spent his life serving our country as a Navy SEAL and in the White House for President Obama. When he retired from the military, he chose to move back to Michigan to raise his family. Matt could have chosen lots of other paths, but he believes that service to the people of Michigan is the most important path he can take.”
Retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam speaks at a candidate forum for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District hosted by the Eaton County Democratic Party and Indivisible Michigan 7th District. April 8, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Maasdam is running in a tight race against former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and Lansing progressive organizer Will Lawrence.
Slotkin’s endorsement gives Maasdam the backing of one of Michigan’s highest-profile Democratic elected officials, and an equally forceful source of opposition against the administration of President Donald Trump.
Slotkin added that Michigan needs “fighters, and whether it is standing up to President Trump’s attacks on our democracy, taking on the corruption and special interests, or standing up for working people,” Maasdam “knows what it means to fight.”
“I look forward to working alongside Matt to win the primary election in August, and then flip this seat in November to re-take the House majority,” Slotkin said.
Maasdam is a retired Navy SEAL who also served as a White House military aide carrying the nuclear codes for former President Barack Obama. Maasdam’s campaign has rejected corporate PAC dollars and calls for banning members of Congress from trading stocks. His platform also calls for lowering costs for families over tax breaks for billionaires and corporations.
He said in a statement that he was “incredibly honored” to have Slotkin’s support, calling her a “singular leader who has shown Democrats in mid-Michigan and across the country how to take on tough fights and win.”
“She never sits back when the stakes are high, and we are lucky to have her fighting for Michigan every day,” Maasdam said of Slotkin. “No one understands this district, its voters, or what it takes to win here better than Senator Slotkin. I’m grateful for her trust in me, and I’m ready to follow her example: fight for every vote, defeat Tom Barrett, flip this seat, and help take back the House so we can put a check on Donald Trump.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Board cites Iowa nurses for meth sales, being under the influence at work, other offenses
description: The Iowa Board of Nursing sanctioned several nurses recently over allegations of being drunk at work, dealing methamphetamine and putting patients at risk. One of the cases involves a nursing home worker, Anita Applegate of Polk County, who was accused of deliberately reusing residents’ insulin-delivery pens on other residents, creating a risk of infection.[...]
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Nursing)The Iowa Board of Nursing sanctioned several nurses recently over allegations of being drunk at work, dealing methamphetamine and putting patients at risk.
One of the cases involves a nursing home worker, Anita Applegate of Polk County, who was accused of deliberately reusing residents’ insulin-delivery pens on other residents, creating a risk of infection.
Applegate, a licensed practical nurse, was recently charged by the Iowa Board of Nursing with failing to properly safeguard or secure medications and with deviating from the standards of skill ordinarily possessed by nurses. The board alleges that Applegate admitted that while working at Royal Oaks Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Urbandale last year, she administered to residents insulin and medications intended for other residents of the home.
In some cases, she allegedly using insulin pens — medical devices that are used to inject insulin using preloaded, premeasured cartridges — that had been previously used by other residents.
According to the board, she did this despite being aware that some residents of the facility had Hepatitis C. She allegedly risked exposing residents to bloodborne viruses, telling one co-worker the facility traditionally reused old insulin pens that would have otherwise been discarded.
The board alleges that Applegate “denies misappropriating medications but did admit to ‘using what was available’ when encountering unusually high glucose levels” in diabetic residents.
State inspection reports indicate that in December 2025, while working at Royal Oaks, Applegate did not dispose of insulin pens from discharged residents and reused them on multiple other residents. Another nurse at the home allegedly told inspectors Applegate instructed her to reuse the pens on other residents because doing so was “saving the company money” and that the practice had been in place since she started working at the home.
According to the inspectors’ reports, Applegate was fired from the facility after the Royal Oaks’ director of nursing was made aware of the practice. The board notes that after working at Royal Oaks, Applegate was employed at Urbandale’s StoryPoint Assisted Living.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Applegate for comment, but state inspectors allege that when they interviewed her, she reported that when she did not have insulin to administer to residents she would “borrow” it from other residents. She allegedly explained she did this during a time when she was working 50 to 70 hours per week and was “on work overload and panicked.”
To settle the disciplinary case, Applegate recently agreed to accept a warning from the Iowa Board of Nursing and agreed to complete 60 hours of educational training on ethics, nursing practice and medication administration.
Other Iowa nurses recently sanctioned by the Board of Nursing include:
Taylor Delude, a registered nurse from Des Moines. According to the board, it fielded a complaint that on Dec. 14, 2025, while working at Select Specialty Hospital in Des Moines, Delude tested positive for alcohol use and was fired five days later. The board alleges she then self-reported to the Iowa Professional Health Program for nurses but subsequently decided she did not want to complete the IPHP program due to expense involved. The board then charged Delude with practicing nursing while under the influence of alcohol. As part of a settlement with the board, Delude has agreed to a six-month suspension of her nursing license, which will be followed by a two-year probationary period that will involve chemical screening and monitoring.
Taylor Lynn Syndergaard, aka Taylor Lynn Miller, a registered nurse who has worked in Alta. Earlier this year, the Board of Nursing charged Syndergaard with obtaining or possessing or administering controlled substances without lawful authority, and with violating an agreement or contract with the Iowa Professional Health Program that assists health professionals with substance abuse issues.
Syndergaard told the Iowa Capital Dispatch she has struggled with an addiction that stems from the prescribed use of opioids. In July 2025, Syndergaard was charged with selling 19 grams of methamphetamine to an individual for $440 in cash and gasoline. She has since pleaded guilty to a charge of intent to manufacture or deliver methamphetamine. Although she has yet to be sentenced, her plea deal with prosecutors contemplates a 10-year suspended prison sentence and four years of probation.
In February 2026, Syndergaard was charged with second-degree theft and criminal mischief. Prosecutors later dismissed the charges, saying evidence gathered during depositions cast doubt on the merits of the state’s case.
Beckee Sue Foss, a registered nurse from central Iowa. According to the board, Foss was working at Des Moines’ Valley View Village on Oct. 7, 2025, when she heard a loud noise and found a resident who had fallen to the floor in his room. She allegedly told a passing certified nursing assistant to go get another nurse to assist the resident, then returned to her desk without performing any examination of the patient and without offering any assistance, leaving the man unattended in his room. The board charged Foss with failing to assess or report the status of a patient.
State inspection reports indicate that on the day in question a CNA at the home entered a male resident’s room and found the man unresponsive and with no pulse. According to the inspectors’ reports, the staff initiated CPR and called 911, after which paramedics intubated the resident despite a do-not-intubate directive in the resident’s medical records at Valley View Village. The resident died, according to state inspection reports.
To settle the disciplinary case, Foss recently agreed to accept a warning from the board and to complete 30 hours of educational training on patient standards of care.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Sen. Dave McCormick: Pennsylvania could be ‘the point of the spear’ in defense innovation
description: Nearly $10 billion in new investment was announced at a two-day summit at the Army War College in Carlisle in the commonwealth’s defense industrial base, emerging technology, research and development and workforce development.
text:
155mm artillery shells in the production shop at the Scranton Army Ammunition Plant on April 12, 2023 in Scranton. (Photo by Hannah Beier/Getty Images)The path of American military history has passed through Pennsylvania during each of the nation’s most consequential conflicts, U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick said Wednesday at the U.S. Army War College in Carlisle. 
The arsenal there supported Gen. George Washington’s army and the hallowed ground of Gettysburg’s battlefield was only about 30 miles away, McCormick noted. 
And during World War II, the commonwealth earned the nickname “the Arsenal of Democracy” as its mines, steel mills and shipyards churned out weapons for the United States and its allies, he said during the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit attended by 600 C-suite executives representing 500 companies.
McCormick’s office announced Wednesday the two-day summit had catalyzed nearly $10 billion in new investment in the commonwealth’s defense industrial base, emerging technology, research and development and workforce development. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
As the nation reaches toward a future where artificial intelligence, robotics, drones and autonomous vehicles play a larger role on the front lines, Pennsylvania is poised to strengthen its position as a base for production and innovation in the defense industry, McCormick said.
The commonwealth has roughly 9,000 defense-related companies that employ 90,000 people supplying materials and parts for cutting edge defense systems, he noted.
“We’re entering a new phase of enormous innovation in defense, and Pennsylvania should be, and in many ways is the point of the spear,” McCormick, a Republican, said in a panel discussion with Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and executives from two prime defense contractors.
Shapiro agreed, adding that along with the state’s traditional defense industries and its academic institutions, the state boasts a strong AI and tech sector. 
Its investments in workforce development and economic growth help to attract new companies, such as South Korean shipbuilder Hanwha Group. The company announced last year it would invest $5 billion in the former Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, where it will eventually build U.S. warships, he said.
Shapiro and McCormick agreed China is the greatest threat to U.S. geopolitical leadership and is moving “too fast” in its development of advanced military technology. The United States needs to work faster to connect the research happening in its universities with tech companies and defense contractors by streamlining its weapons procurement process.
The governor warned that the isolationist policies of the Trump administration threaten to cut it off from its trading and military partners, who are force-multipliers in the fight to stay ahead of the United States’ rivals. 
“I get a little bit concerned when our administration pokes their finger in the eye of our allies,” Shapiro said. “That undermines our ability to innovate, and it undermines our ability to be stronger with our national defense and to have a deterrence that is going to protect the American people and protect our interests abroad.”
A member of the National Guard stands alongside a military vehicle parked in front of Union Station, near the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Monday, Aug. 18, 2025. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)
The Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit is the second gathering of industry, academic and government leaders that McCormick and his wife, Meta president Dina Powell McCormick, have organized. Last July, they hosted a summit on energy and artificial intelligence in Pittsburgh.
The two-day event at the War College was headlined by President Donald Trump, who was to conclude the gathering Wednesday afternoon.
The event featured exhibits by defense contractors ranging from General Dynamics, which operates a munitions plant in northeast Pennsylvania, to small robotics and drone developers.
Michael Coulter, president and CEO of Hanwha Defense USA, said that by working with the Trump administration, the state and city government, the company has plans to double the size of its footprint and has more than doubled its workforce with plans to hire up to 10,000 people.
Hanwha has already invested more than $200 million in the shipyard, which is more than the facility has since the second world war, Coulter said.
“So we are ‘foot on the throttle’ to make shipbuilding great again, and Pennsylvania is the heart of that,” he said.
General Dynamics employs 2,200 people in eight operations in the commonwealth, company President Danny Deep said. But what makes the company’s presence here unique is the diversity of the operations. 
They include the Scranton Army Munitions Plant, where the company nearly quadrupled its production of 155 mm Howitzer shells to 50,000 a month to support Ukranian forces in the war with Russia. That expansion was the result of a $500 million investment from the U.S. government, he said. 
Both Coulter and Deep said a workforce trained in skilled trades like welders, boilermakers, and electricians are crucial both to maintaining the nation’s status as a defense leader. It was a theme repeated by other speakers throughout Wednesday’s program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But companies like Hanwha are also focused on the workforce of the future, which will be heavily involved in automation and robotics. Coulter said. 
“People mistake automation and robotics with the lack of jobs or replacing jobs. I can tell you, our shipyard in Korea, we have 30,000 workers, and it is very highly automated,” Coulter said, adding that getting students onto a vocational or technical career track is crucial.
Shapiro noted Pennsylvania has drawn 43,000 high school students into career and technical education to learn skilled trades.
Penn State President Neeli Bendapudi, who moderated the discussion, asked the panelists what is their greatest concern about national security.
Deep, of General Dynamics, said it’s complacency about the state of geopolitics. 
“I think there has been a real call to action over the last number of years as we’ve seen these conflicts around the world proliferate and the threat environment get worse and worse,” he said. “At the end of the day, there’s a monopsony buyer, and so the threat environment dictates the policy environment, and the policy environment dictates the budget environment, and the budget environment will either attract players into this field or it won’t.”
McCormick said the threat from China depends on how the nation moves forward with its defense policy, noting the Department of War must undergo dramatic changes. Strategic resources such as rare earth metals must be treated as a national security issue. And the nation needs a workforce that can meet the moment. 
“It’s like a symphony. All the different parts have to work together,” he said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State CFO tapped to run Oklahoma Health Care Authority
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s CFO will lead the state’s Health Care Authority after the current director said he would be stepping down after less than a year in the role.  Gov. Kevin Stitt on Wednesday announced he had appointed Aaron Morris, the chief financial officer for the state of Oklahoma, to be the interim director […]
text:
State Chief Financial Officer Aaron Morris attends a news conference announcing details of the Fiscal Year 2027 state budget on April 1, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s CFO will lead the state’s Health Care Authority after the current director said he would be stepping down after less than a year in the role. 
Gov. Kevin Stitt on Wednesday announced he had appointed Aaron Morris, the chief financial officer for the state of Oklahoma, to be the interim director of the agency, which administers the state’s Medicaid program. Morris will serve in the role for the remainder of Stitt’s term as governor. 
Stitt said Clay Bullard, the current director, said he planned to return to the private sector. Bullard was appointed as director in October, following experience as a healthcare executive and consultant. 
Clay Bullard was appointed as the director of the Oklahoma Health Care Authority on Oct. 3, 2025. (Photo provided by the Governor’s Office)
Morris has served as the state CFO since 2024. Prior to that, he spent 20 years working at the Health Care Authority, six of which were as the agency’s CFO. 
He has a bachelor’s degree in finance from the University of Central Oklahoma and an MBA from Cameron University. 
“It is a privilege to continue serving my state, and I am grateful for the Governor’s confidence in me,” Morris said in a statement. “I look forward to returning to OHCA and to working to address the budgetary and regulatory issues that face the agency.”
The Health Care Authority requested nearly half a billion dollars from the Legislature to adjust for changes in the federal dollars coming to the state and address cash flow issues, but was appropriated $250 million. The state attorney general also requested an audit of the agency and said the Health Care Authority hasn’t adequately held accountable some of the companies who administer Oklahoma’s privatized  Medicaid program, known as managed care. 
It was not immediately clear when Morris would step into the role, nor when Bullard’s last day would be but Bullard will “provide leadership transition support over the coming weeks,” according to a news release. 
Stitt said he is grateful that Morris agreed to step into the director role and said he is a trusted member of his team. 
“Aaron has proved to be a steady leader through any challenge,” Stitt said in a statement. “As CFO of the State, he has worked carefully to protect our state’s savings, navigate complicated budget issues, and assist agencies to increase accountability and transparency.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Have a felony record in Alaska? You may still be eligible to vote.
description: Alaska’s midterm election season is underway. Residents who lost the right to vote with a felony conviction may have their right restored once they are unconditionally discharged from the Alaska Department of Corrections’ supervision. Restoration of voting rights after a felony conviction varies by state. Alaska is one of more than a dozen states that […]
text:
A ballot and instructions for the 2024 Alaska primary election are seen on Monday, Aug. 5, 2024. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Alaska’s midterm election season is underway. Residents who lost the right to vote with a felony conviction may have their right restored once they are unconditionally discharged from the Alaska Department of Corrections’ supervision.
Restoration of voting rights after a felony conviction varies by state. Alaska is one of more than a dozen states that requires residents to complete their prison sentence and be unconditionally discharged from custody before their right to vote is restored. 
That means Alaskans can vote again once they are no longer under DOC supervision, which includes halfway houses, sentenced electronic monitoring, probation or parole.
The Department of Corrections is required to issue a letter as proof of unconditional discharge, which residents must provide to the Alaska Division of Elections to re-register to vote if they otherwise meet eligibility requirements. 
The deadline to register to vote is July 19 for Alaska’s primary elections, September 6 for local elections and October 4 for the midterm elections in November. 
Residents can check their voter registration at myvoterportal.alaska.gov.
Alaskans lose the right to vote after a state or federal felony conviction involving crimes of moral turpitude, a list which includes murder, assault, drug-related felonies and others. That means they are ineligible to vote in all local, state and federal elections while in prison and under DOC supervision.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

If convicted of a misdemeanor or a felony not involving a crime of moral turpitude, Alaskans are eligible to register and vote in elections. 
The roughly 40% of Alaska’s incarcerated population who is pre-trial — even under felony charges — are also eligible to vote. That includes incarcerated Alaskans who are awaiting trial, plea agreements or sentencing.
This year, the deadline for eligible voters to apply for absentee by-mail voting is August 8 for the primary, and by October 24 for the general election. 
An official with the Department of Corrections said probation officers at all correctional facilities will assist any inmate that requests help with voting, including registration, updating address information and applying for or casting an absentee ballot. 
“Each facility has posted in all common areas an instructional notice from the Division of Elections and each facility has paper copies of the absentee ballot application,” said Betsy Holley, a public information officer for the department, by email on Wednesday. 
Under Alaska statute, most inmate mail is scanned and copied before it is provided to inmates. Ballots are considered “privileged mail” and subject to monitoring under specific criteria, Holley said. Inmates fill out their ballots and cast their vote like any other eligible voter. 
“Mailroom staff may not read or search outgoing privileged mail. Mailroom staff will verify, in the prisoner’s presence, that the intended recipient of the mail is the same person as the privileged addressee,” Holley said. 
Holley said the numbers of Alaskans unconditionally discharged from DOC custody and eligible to vote each year was not immediately available. 
The ACLU of Alaska has updated voter guidance and resources for formerly and currently incarcerated Alaskans. The organization, along with state nonprofit Partners for Progress, is hosting voter restoration information sessions this election season.
“Incarceration does not automatically disqualify Alaskans from voting,” said Meghan Barker, ACLU of Alaska communications director, by email on Tuesday. “It’s critical that people who have interacted with the criminal legal system know their rights and know how to either request an absentee ballot while incarcerated or, if eligible, take the steps to restore their voting rights after they’ve been incarcerated.”
Barker said that as of May  there are nearly 1,750 Alaskans that are incarcerated and awaiting trial or sentencing that may be eligible to vote. She noted that Alaska Native people make up a disproportionate number of those incarcerated statewide. While Alaska Native people are less than 20% of the state’s population, they made up 40% of the prison population last year.
“As we continue to look at ways to combat the disenfranchisement of Alaska Native people, we must also consider the demographics of Alaska’s prisons and the people who are eligible to vote, even if they are incarcerated far from their home communities or districts where they would vote,” she said.
