title: After 2 deadly shootings, ICE reportedly ordered to end vehicle enforcement stops
text: WASHINGTON — The Department of Homeland Security Tuesday ordered U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to cease vehicle-related enforcement stops, following the deadly shootings of two men in their vehicles, according to multiple media reports. A DHS spokesperson did not respond directly to States Newsroom’s question about what was characterized in some reports as a new nationwide order. “We are always evaluating our procedures to keep our officers safe and criminals off our streets,” the spokesperson said. “We will not disclose or discuss law enforcement tactics.”U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican who is up for reelection in one of the nation’s most closely watched races, said on social media Tuesday that she spoke with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Monday night and “urged him to cease all non-urgent vehicle stops.” ICE officers killed a 26-year-old Colombian man with legal status in his vehicle in Biddeford, Maine, on Monday.As the Trump administration aims to carry out mass deportations, aggressive enforcement has occurred across the interior of the country, with at least 21 shootings involving federal immigration agents. At least 10 of those incidents have been deadly.Monday’s shooting in Maine, coupled with another by federal immigration officers who on July 7 killed 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national, during a traffic stop in Houston, Texas, renewed congressional anger and demand for answers. Neither man was an initial person of interest for immigration enforcement, DHS stated.Hispanic Caucus calls for abolishing ICEOn Tuesday, the Congressional Hispanic Caucus condemned federal immigration agents for the recent shootings, calling for congressional oversight and for the dismantling of ICE.“An agency that acts as though it is above the law cannot be reformed at the margins,” said New York Democrat Nydia Velázquez. “You cannot put a Band-Aid on a system that is fundamentally broken. We must abolish ICE.”“Here we are again, a brown man, a Latino, killed,” said the chair of the Hispanic Caucus, Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York.Members of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus said the recent killings are a pattern with immigration enforcement under the Trump administration, coupled with conflicting statements given by the Department of Homeland Security and independent video recordings of the incidents. The department came under intense scrutiny after federal immigration officers shot and killed two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January, Renee Good and Alex Pretti. Minnesota prosecutors announced Monday that they started receiving evidence from the federal government about their killings after the Trump administration initially refused to turn over evidence to local law enforcement. Espaillat said members of the Hispanic Caucus will hold a field hearing in Houston on July 24 with House Democrats on the Homeland Security Committee. Democrats plan to focus the hearing on the killing of Salgado Araujo, a construction worker, husband and father of three U.S. citizen children. ICE to get billionsTexas Democrat Joaquin Castro said that Congress must not only use its power of subpoena to conduct oversight, but must freeze hiring at ICE and refuse to fund the agency. Congressional Republicans funded ICE and Border Patrol with $70 billion until September 2029 through a special legislative process after Democrats refused to fund DHS for fiscal year 2026. Additionally, congressional Republicans last year approved roughly $170 billion for DHS to conduct immigration enforcement and hire more ICE and Border Patrol agents.“We have to disband ICE in this Congress,” Castro said. “Otherwise, these killings will continue. There will be another victim in a few days or a few weeks.” Texas Democratic Rep. Sylvia Garcia said she has a meeting with Homeland Security’s Mullin this week, where she plans to ask questions related to the Texas and Maine shootings. “This is a human life,” she said of Salgado Araujo. “He was not the target. He had no criminal record. He may not even be the right man. Those are very troubling questions for everybody.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Environmental group drops ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ pollution suit after site shuts down
description: An environmental group seeking to punish state operators of the “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration lockup for alleged pollution of the Florida Everglades has withdrawn its case, the Center for Biological Diversity announced Monday. Because the nation’s first state-run migrant detention center is fully closed, the environmental nonprofit says, its goal has been[...]
text:
Protesters line the highway outside Alligator Alcatraz (Photo via Jessica Namath).An environmental group seeking to punish state operators of the “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration lockup for alleged pollution of the Florida Everglades has withdrawn its case, the Center for Biological Diversity announced Monday.
Because the nation’s first state-run migrant detention center is fully closed, the environmental nonprofit says, its goal has been accomplished and there’s no need to continue its federal lawsuit.
“We achieved the desired result with our Clean Air Act lawsuit. This detestable facility’s air pollution will not continue,” Ryan Maher, a staff attorney at the center, said in a written statement.
The center filed the case two months ago in the federal Southern District of Florida, alleging the detention center was emitting hundreds of tons of toxic gases into the atmosphere without a permit, flouting the Clean Air Act, and demanded more than $120,000 per environmental violation per day.
It alleged the site’s 100 diesel-powered lighting towers and up to 200 diesel-powered generators — employed without a special air quality permit — consumed nearly 8 million gallons of fuel on an annualized basis and emitted hundreds of tons of carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides.
But the June closure of the facility, officially cleared out last weekend, has brought an end to any potential air pollution. Gov. Ron DeSantis confirmed last month that the center had been emptied of detainees and was being torn down. This came on the heels of persistent, weeks-long rumors that officials were quietly planning to end the temporary facility — which saw more than 22,000 detainees in its 11-month lifespan — despite federal and state authorities denying any “official” closure talks were taking place.
Despite this, the center vowed that its legal battles with the state are far from over.
“The fight continues to ensure that the site is fully remediated and the Trump and DeSantis administrations are held accountable,” Maher said.
He referred to another suit against the state brought by the center and environmental groups including Friends of the Everglades, the Miccosukee Tribe, and Earthjustice. That case alleged that Florida violated the National Environmental Policy Act in constructing the facility because they failed to complete a federal environmental study ahead of building.
First filed in June 2025, mere days after work began on the Everglades site, the case has ping-ponged across the state — with vastly different results. At first, a federal trial judge in Miami sided with the advocates and ordered the facility quickly torn down and deactivated.
But a federal appellate court in April found that the facility didn’t have to comply with federal environmental law because it was entirely state-run and — at the time — lacked federal funding. That three-judge panel kicked the case back to the lower court, which is expected to reexamine the matter sometime this summer.
The federal dollars referred to in the court decision involves a $608 million reimbursement long promised to Florida for operating the facility. At the time of the ruling, the state had received nothing but vague assurances that the money would come. In May, officials received the first $58 million tranche.
“We and our partners will not stop until every piece of infrastructure tied to this facility is gone for good, the damage is assessed, and Big Cypress is restored,” Maher added.

title: Restraint chair ‘will be disposed of’ when civil rights lawsuit is over, Wyoming Boys’ School leadership says
description:
State youth prison hasn’t used restraint chair since 2022, figures from the Department of Family Services show
The post Restraint chair ‘will be disposed of’ when civil rights lawsuit is over, Wyoming Boys’ School leadership says appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The restraint chair at the center of a lawsuit alleging abuse at the Wyoming Boys’ School “will be disposed of” when litigation is over, the Wyoming Department of Family Services said in a statement to WyoFile. 
According to department figures, the chair hasn’t been used on residents since 2022. It currently remains at the school, “but only for the purpose of preserving evidence per the lawsuit,” the department said. 
In 2024, six former boys’ school residents joined a lawsuit alleging abuse at the facility, including extended periods of solitary confinement and physical harm. The school, where judges can sentence delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre facility near Worland overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services.
In June, the former residents filed a court document that included an image — which sparked outrage on social media — of one of the plaintiffs in a restraint chair with a bag over his head. Images included in the filing show that the chair bears a warning label that states: “Warning: Use of the safety restraint chair without first reading and thoroughly understanding the instructions could cause injury or death. . . Do not leave detainees in this chair for more than TWO hours.”
Photos from a court filing show a resident alone in solitary confinement and another strapped to a restraint chair with hood over his head at Wyoming Boys’ School. (Court filing)
Despite the warning, some of the former residents allege that the school put them in the restraint chair for more than two hours. In 2021, Dale Weber, the school’s superintendent, approved restraining one of the plaintiffs in the chair from 11:50 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., according to the document. Another former resident was restrained in the chair for about five hours in 2019, the document states. 
The school purchased the high-back chair, which has shoulder, lap, wrist and ankle straps, in 2016. Use of the chair climbed from once in 2018 to 23 times in 2021, according to figures from the family services department. Allegations in the lawsuit stem from that time period. 
The number of times the restraint chair was used dropped in 2022, the first decrease since the school started using the chair in 2018. The school hasn’t used the chair since then, according to the Department of Family Services. 
The department handles allegations of abuse or mistreatment at the boys’ school as Child Protective Services cases. Such cases are confidential under statute, according to Wyoming Department of Family Services Director Korin Schmidt. Child Protective Services is part of the family services department, meaning the agency itself investigates allegations against the boys’ school, which it oversees, without external oversight or transparency. 
The department said in a statement to Wyofile that it doesn’t work with third-party, independent investigators when looking into complaints at the boys’ school. 
Most of the defendants, including Weber, continue to work at the boys’ school, employee rosters show. Defendants Mark Nelson, Kevin McGinty and Darryl Coronado no longer work at the school. 
Since October, Weber has also served as the interim superintendent of the Wyoming Girls’ School after long-time superintendent Chris Jones retired, according to the Department of Family Services. 
WyoFile editor Tennessee Watson contributed to this story.

title: High temps and high winds: What to know about Vermont’s possible severe weather today
description:
The National Weather Service is forecasting enhanced risk of severe thunderstorms this evening and tonight.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  High temps and high winds: What to know about Vermont’s possible severe weather today.
text:
The entire state of Vermont is under a heat advisory, with the heat index expected to reach above 100 degrees in the Champlain Valley and portions of southeastern Vermont. 
Vermont is expecting a triple threat of heat, wildfire smoke and severe storms — including the possibility of tornadoes — from Tuesday afternoon into Tuesday night and possibly beyond, the National Weather Service reported.
The weather service has taken the rare step of issuing an “enhanced risk” designation for severe thunderstorms in northern Vermont, particularly in the Northeast Kingdom, said Tyler Danvig, a meteorologist for the weather service.  
“The last time we had an enhanced risk anywhere in the state of Vermont was 2024, and that was for southern Vermont,” he said. 
That means conditions are favorable for multiple types of hazards: high winds up to 70 or 75 mph, hail and tornadoes. Danvig cautioned there was still a lot of uncertainty about where and how severely the storms would hit. 
“Models typically do not do very well” with the kind of cold front and convective air patterns expected tonight, he said. “It’s hard for them to understand how things are currently going since they evolve very quickly.”
What looks likely is that the severe weather will begin sometime past sunset, with the greatest risk happening between sunset and midnight. Danvig said his greatest concern was for people camping in the northern end of the state who may not be aware of what’s happening as it unfolds. 
“Cell service might not be that great, and with the terrain, you may not see things coming,” he said. “We want to stress people to be weather aware before they go to bed tonight, or have a plan in place for evacuations or for safety precautions later this evening into the overnight period.” 
If you start to experience high winds or lightning while camping, Danvig advised moving to a sturdy building or your vehicle. While significant flooding isn’t in the forecast, he said people should stay away from water sources as much as possible to avoid small-scale, localized flash flooding. 
He added that people at home should close their windows to prevent pressure buildup that could shatter glass. People should move away from windows into a more secure place in their homes if winds get particularly severe, he advised. 
Regardless of location, people should consider charging their phones, turning on Wireless Emergency Alerts and keeping a flashlight handy, he said.  
Heat advisory in effect
The entire state of Vermont is under a heat advisory, with the heat index expected to reach above 100 degrees in the Champlain Valley and portions of southeastern Vermont. Danvig said the heat is only expected to last for one day, making it a little less severe than the heat wave Vermont experienced earlier this summer. 
However, the state is also receiving wildfire smoke blowing in from western and central Canada. Most of the smoke is stuck in the upper atmosphere, lessening its effect on air quality, but sensitive groups should still be cautious and keep an eye on the air quality forecast, Danvig said. 
“It remains a little unclear right now how the current wildfire environment is going to affect our thunderstorm potential,” he said. 
The smoke lowers temperatures, but it also helps water condense, which could end up increasing the storm risk. 
The weather service will have a better idea of that risk as it gets closer to nighttime, Danvig said. 
“We’re going to have to pay attention to how the environment is changing this afternoon before the storms actually get to us,” he said. 
This story will be updated.

name: Delaware
title: A Re-Cap of the Major Legislation that Cleared the General Assembly and the Bills That Stalled.
description: Delaware lawmakers closed the 153rd General Assembly in a marathon overnight session that stretched into the early morning of July 1, sending Gov. Matt Meyer major spending bills and a long list of policy measures while leaving several high-profile proposals to die with the end of the two-year session. The final hours produced a nearly $7 billion operating b[...]
text:
Delaware lawmakers closed the 153rd General Assembly in a marathon overnight session that stretched into the early morning of July 1, sending Gov. Matt Meyer major spending bills and a long list of policy measures while leaving several high-profile proposals to die with the end of the two-year session.
The final hours produced a nearly $7 billion operating budget, a roughly $1.25 billion capital budget, about $99 million in grant-in-aid funding and action on issues ranging from voting access and marriage protections to wetlands, marijuana zoning, energy policy, gun regulation and property tax fallout.
The session also showed the limits of last-day legislating. Bills addressing child sexual abuse claims, reproductive freedom, privacy rights, union labor requirements, broader pension tax relief, tobacco taxes and several election changes failed to make it across the finish line and would need to be reintroduced when a new General Assembly convenes in January 2027.
Voting rights measures advance, but not all survive
Election policy was one of the clearest themes of the closing stretch. Lawmakers advanced constitutional amendments that would authorize early in-person voting, expand absentee voting without requiring an excuse, bar corporations and other artificial entities from voting in Delaware elections, and restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies once they are released from incarceration or pardoned. Because most of those measures are constitutional amendments, they must pass again in the next General Assembly before taking effect.
A separate voting rights bill, the Delaware John Lewis Voting Rights Act, cleared the legislature and headed to Meyer’s desk. The measure would create state-level protections against voter suppression, vote dilution, intimidation and barriers facing voters whose first language is not English.
Other election proposals stalled. A plan to move Delaware’s primary date to April, an open primaries bill for unaffiliated voters, a proposal to let voters approve constitutional amendments directly and a measure allowing voters to cast ballots at any polling place in their county all failed to advance before adjournment.
Budgets, infrastructure and late-session disputes
The budget package anchored the final day. Meyer signed the operating budget before lawmakers completed work on the capital budget and grant-in-aid bill. The bond bill funded public construction, school projects, transportation and other infrastructure, but it drew scrutiny over spending levels and transparency in the early-morning rush.
Days later, Meyer used a line-item veto to remove $35 million for a Legislative Hall expansion from the capital plan, saying the expense could not be justified amid affordability concerns. The rest of the bond bill remained intact, but the veto underscored tension between the new administration and legislative leaders over priorities and fiscal restraint.
Social policy fights end with mixed results
Some of the most closely watched social-policy proposals ended unresolved. A constitutional amendment on reproductive freedom, a constitutional right-to-privacy proposal and a bill criticized by opponents as restricting anti-abortion advocacy did not receive final approval before adjournment. Their failure was celebrated by conservative and faith-based advocacy groups, while supporters would need to restart the measures in a new session.
A separate bill intended to expand legal options for survivors of child sexual abuse also collapsed after the Senate amended it and the House declined to accept the revised version. Advocates who supported the original bill said the amendment weakened the measure too much to accomplish its purpose.
Lawmakers did advance the first leg of a constitutional amendment protecting marriage regardless of gender or race, a measure that will also need approval in the next General Assembly.
Other major bills clear the finish line
Beyond budgets and elections, legislators approved measures on data center regulation, wetlands permitting, campaign finance, gun dealer oversight, housing, property tax administration and marijuana business zoning. They also overrode Meyer’s earlier veto of legislation limiting the land-use restrictions counties can impose on recreational marijuana retailers.
The late-night schedule frustrated some lawmakers, who complained that major bills and Senate amendments arrived with little time for review. Legislative leaders, however, described the rush as a familiar feature of June in Dover, when unresolved negotiations often pile up at the deadline.
What comes next
Because the 153rd General Assembly has ended, ordinary bills that failed are dead for now. Many ideas are expected to return next year, when all House seats and several Senate seats will be on the ballot and the next legislature may look different from the one that adjourned before sunrise.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: ‘We are America’: Chelsea named All-America city for the second year in a row
description: Nearly half of Chelsea’s predominantly Latino population was born outside of the United States — the largest foreign-born population of any community in Massachusetts. The city’s award application highlighted its community-centered policing, food distribution system, and youth development initiatives – efforts that have helped strengthen residents’ trust in[...]
text:
THIS YEAR’S THEME for the National Civic League’s “All-America” city awards was “America at 250 – Strengthening Civic Health and Building Trust.”
That apparently gave Chelsea a winning edge, as the immigrant-rich city of 40,000 was one of 10 US cities selected for the award, announced two weeks ago. It was the second year in a row the city was selected for the award.
Nearly half of Chelsea’s predominantly Latino population was born outside of the United States — the largest foreign-born population of any community in Massachusetts. The city’s award application highlighted its community-centered policing, food distribution system, and youth development initiatives – efforts that have helped strengthen residents’ trust in local government amid a federal immigration crackdown that has had Chelsea in its crosshairs, according to city officials.
Tying that kind of trust-building among immigrants in government to the country’s semiquincentennial celebration is not quite the picture of America at 250 projected by President Trump, who has a long track record of disparaging immigrants, and injected a strong nativist edge to the anniversary observance.
“There is now a resurgence of the communist menace in our land, including from newcomers to our country who embrace ideas totally opposed to our way of life and our great success,” Trump said during a July 3 speech at Mount Rushmore.
Chelsea – a sanctuary city and a first home for many immigrants in the Greater Boston area – has long been at odds with the Trump administration and its policies.
Shortly after his inauguration in 2025, Trump issued executive orders threatening to cut off federal funds to sanctuary cities. Chelsea then sued the administration in February 2025 in an effort to avoid aiding federal immigration authorities in arrests and deportations. A month later, the city was the focus of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement raid.  
“Chelsea is the ultimate underdog. We’re always fighting forces that are bigger than us, and last year was a very hard year,” City Manager Fidel Maltez said. “When immigration enforcement is so visible in the community, we have to reassure residents that they can trust our police department, and they can trust our government.”
When he was appointed in 2023, Maltez, who immigrated to the US from Nicaragua when he was seven years old, became Chelsea’s first Latino city manager.
“We are America,” Maltez said. “I hear and feel the most patriotism from our immigrant communities. We are excited to be a part of this country, we are excited to work on it each and every day, and we know that nothing is owed to us.”
A street mural in Chelsea. (Photo by Bhaamati Borkhetaria)
This year, the All-America designation – rarely given to a community two years in a row – honored cities that “bring the ideal of a government of, by, and for the people to life,” according to the civic league.
Following the murder of George Floyd in 2020 and during federal immigration enforcement actions in 2025, the Chelsea Police Department, in an effort to increase trust, coordinated a downtown task force and facilitated ongoing “Faith & Blue” events that connect officers with residents through faith-based gatherings.
The department also strengthened its Community Services Division by embedding officers in schools and housing communities. It continues to host programs like Cops and Bobbers, an opportunity for Chelsea youth to go fishing with an officer, and Build the Base, a youth camp hosted by officers that focuses on discipline, leadership, mental health, and positive engagement between youth and law enforcement.
“It might seem like a silly program, but it’s how trust is built,” Maltez said of Cops and Bobbers. “It’s beautiful to see young people of color out on the water with our police officers.”
During the height of the pandemic, the city experienced one of the worst COVID outbreaks in Massachusetts. Food insecurity was prevalent, and undocumented families who were ineligible for government safety nets like SNAP were especially vulnerable. In response, the city implemented a food distribution system consisting of neighborhood-based pickup sites and home delivery services through a 311-request system, which provided access to food during the crisis and was a lifeline for immigrants, low-income workers, and non-English speakers.
Nearly 21 percent of the city’s residents live below the poverty line, compared to about 10 percent across Massachusetts and 11 percent nationwide.
Another local initiative highlighted in Chelsea’s All-America city application is aimed at addressing high dropout risk among overage, under-credited, multilingual, and working students. Chelsea Public Schools created an alternative high school in 2018 called the Chelsea Opportunity Academy. The academy is competency-based rather than attendance-based and offers flexible scheduling, replacing traditional grading and disciplinary systems that have long prevented disadvantaged students, including those of color, from graduating. The school, in addition to having bilingual staff, facilitates mentoring, home visits, and daily check-ins.
Prior to winning the title in 2025 for its community-led sustainability practices, Chelsea had been named an All-America city twice before — once in 1998 and again in 2014. 
“We want to show that the concept of America is a road,” Maltez said. “It’s a process, and it’s a journey. We celebrate the win, but we know that there’s a lot of work left to do for everyone in our community.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: After entering the country 10 years ago at age 11, Iowa man is detained by ICE
description: A federal judge has intervened in the case of an Iowa man jailed by ICE after living in the United States for 10 years since the age of 11. Alvaro Anastacio Garcia Tevalan of Clarion recently filed a federal lawsuit against Polk County Chief Jail Administrator Cory Williams, Acting Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs […]
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is holding dozens of individuals in Iowa jails. (Main photo by Caspar Benson/Getty Images; logo courtesy U.S. Department of Homeland Security)  A federal judge has intervened in the case of an Iowa man jailed by ICE after living in the United States for 10 years since the age of 11.
Alvaro Anastacio Garcia Tevalan of Clarion recently filed a federal lawsuit against Polk County Chief Jail Administrator Cory Williams, Acting Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement David Venturella, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, and Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche. Tevalan’s lawsuit challenged the legality of his current detention by ICE, seeking either his immediate release or a court hearing at which he could argue for temporary release on bond.
Court records show that Tevalan, who is a citizen of Guatemala, entered the United States without authorization in November 2016 at the age of 11. He was apprehended by Border Patrol agents who processed him as a minor unaccompanied by an adult and immediately placed him with the Office of Refugee Resettlement. Within a few weeks, the government released him to his mother’s custody in Clarion, Iowa.
Now 20 years old, Tevalan has lived in the United States for almost 10 years and has a child who is a United States citizen. Court records indicate he has never violated the terms of his release in 2016.
On April 29, 2026, Tevalan was arrested in Wright County on a charge of domestic-abuse assault. Police alleged he was involved in an altercation with the female victim, who was left with scratches or bruises on her arms and shoulders.
An ICE officer then lodged a detainer against Tevalan, and ICE took custody of him on May 1, 2026, and he has allegedly remained in jail since that time. The domestic abuse charge remains pending, with a Wright County judge having entered a June 18 warrant for Tevalan’s arrest for failing to appear for a trial hearing in the case. Court records indicate that due to the ICE detainer, Tevalan was in the Polk County Jail at that time of the planned hearing.
Chief Judge Stephanie M. Rose of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa. (Photo courtesy U.S. District Court)
Recently, Stephanie Rose, chief judge for the U.S. District Court of the Southern District of Iowa, took up Tevalan’s lawsuit seeking his immediate release or a bond hearing. The question before the court, Rose ruled, was “whether the government may re-detain, without process, a noncitizen it allowed to live at liberty in the country for nearly a decade. It may not.”
While the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals has held that under federal law noncitizens who enter the country without authorization and are later arrested are subjected to mandatory detention, Rose said that decision “does not end the matter” in Tevalan’s case, where constitutional rights are at play.
Rose concluded that the government, having released Tevalan and allowed him to live at liberty for a decade, cannot now re-detain him without due process.
“When the government releases a noncitizen into the country and allows him to remain, it does more than perform an administrative gesture,” Rose ruled. “It permits him to order his life around his continued liberty, and over time that reliance ripens into an interest the due-process clause protects. A person permitted to remain at liberty receives an implicit promise that their liberty will be revoked only if they fail to live up to the conditions of release.”
The due process protections of the Constitution are guaranteed to all persons within the United States, including Tevalan, Rose stated.
“He has lived in the United States for nearly a decade and raised a citizen child,” Rose stated. “For all those years the government left him at liberty, and until his recent arrest, it alleged no breach of the terms of his release …  For a decade the government allowed (Tevalan) to live in the community, and in all that time it never alleged he broke a term of his release.”
Rose also noted that whether Tevalan’s April 2026 arrest makes him ineligible for release on bond is a question for an immigration judge to decide at a bond hearing, which Rose ordered while declining Tevalan’s request for immediate release.

title: Discover the Art of Flight Without Leaving Delaware at Ascend Flow Arts
description: Ascend Flow Arts has introduced hundreds of Delawareans to the world of aerial arts, acrobatics, and creative movement. By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE News For anyone who has ever watched an aerial performance and wondered what it would be like to soar through the air, a Wilmington studio is making that dream far more accessible than[...]
text:
Ascend Flow Arts has introduced hundreds of Delawareans to the world of aerial arts, acrobatics, and creative movement.
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE News
For anyone who has ever watched an aerial performance and wondered what it would be like to soar through the air, a Wilmington studio is making that dream far more accessible than many people realize.
Since opening its doors in the spring of 2014, Ascend Flow Arts has introduced hundreds of Delawareans to the world of aerial arts, acrobatics, and creative movement. Located in Wilmington, the studio welcomes students of all ages and experience levels, proving that aerial fitness is not reserved for professional performers or former gymnasts.
Instead, it is a place where beginners, families, and experienced movers alike can build strength, confidence, and artistic expression in a supportive environment.
According to information on the Ascend Flow Arts website, the studio’s mission is to “create a second home for students where they are free to embrace their love of movement and artistic expression through high quality instruction in a welcoming community.”
That philosophy is reflected in a wide variety of classes designed for children, teens, and adults.
For adults, the journey often begins with an introductory aerial workshop where participants can experience aerial silks, sling, static trapeze, and aerial hoop without making a long-term commitment. From there, students can continue with structured classes that gradually develop strength, flexibility, coordination, and confidence.
The studio emphasizes that no previous dance, gymnastics, or fitness experience is required to get started.
For those who may be intimidated by the thought of leaving the ground, Ascend works to make the experience approachable. Beginner classes are conducted close to the floor using padded gymnastics flooring, crash mats, and carefully supervised instruction designed to help students progress safely.
The studio also offers ground-based movement programs that include Acro Dance and partner acrobatics. These classes blend dance, flexibility, tumbling, balance, and strength while helping students develop body awareness that can complement aerial training or stand on its own as a rewarding fitness activity.
Young students have their own pathways as well.
Children as young as four can begin with Pre-Acrodance classes that introduce ballet and acrobatic fundamentals through games and age-appropriate instruction. As students grow, they can advance into youth aerial and acrobatics programs that focus on developing both technical skills and personal growth.
According to the website, the studio believes it teaches much more than circus arts.
“We don’t just teach circus, we teach life skills through circus,” the website states. “Kids classes have an emphasis on socialization, teamwork, confidence building, discipline, and strength, all while having a great time and learning new skills.”
Those life lessons continue throughout the youth curriculum, where instructors emphasize patience, kindness, focus, emotional regulation, and teamwork alongside physical development.
Class sizes are intentionally kept small, typically between six and eight students, allowing instructors to provide individualized coaching and adapt lessons to each student’s experience level.
Safety remains a central focus throughout every program. Equipment is routinely inspected, students follow a structured curriculum, and instructors carefully guide participants through each stage of progression before introducing more advanced skills.
Ascend also offers supervised open practice sessions for enrolled students, giving them additional opportunities to refine techniques outside of regular classes while remaining in a safe training environment.
Beyond fitness, many participants discover something unexpected.
The combination of movement, creativity, problem-solving, and personal achievement creates an experience that is as mentally rewarding as it is physically challenging. Whether mastering a first climb on aerial silks, balancing in a handstand, or completing a new sequence on the trapeze, students often celebrate accomplishments they never imagined possible.
More than a decade after opening, Ascend Flow Arts continues introducing Delaware residents to a unique form of exercise that combines athleticism with artistry, creating a welcoming community where students of every age can literally and figuratively reach new heights.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Federal judge dismisses lawsuit against West Virginia over voter data
description: A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice against West Virginia over access to unredacted voter registration information.
text:
West Virginia Secretary of State Kris Warner has been sued by the U.S. Department of Justice for refusing to turn over voter records. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice against West Virginia over access to unredacted voter registration information. 
The federal government has demanded sensitive voter registration data in nearly every state and Washington D.C. 
The DOJ’s Civil Rights Division filed the lawsuit against West Virginia and four other states in February. The lawsuit against West Virginia named Secretary of State Kris Warner in his official capacity. 
It argued that the U.S. attorney general has authority to request election records under the Civil Rights Act of 1960. The law allows the attorney general “to demand the production, inspection, and analysis of statewide voter registration lists that can be cross-checked effectively for improper registrations,” a news release at the time said. 
According to the Brennan Center, the federal government altogether sued more than 30 states and Washington D.C. for not complying with requests to turn over the voter registration information, including driver’s license numbers and partial social security numbers. Thirteen of the lawsuits have been dismissed. 
“Clearly, (the DOJ’s demand for data)  is devoid of any factual basis,” U.S. District Judge Thomas Johnston wrote a 16-page order filed Monday. “The demand includes no indication that West Virginia is suspected to be noncompliant with the list maintenance requirements of (Help America Vote Act) or the (National Voter Registration Act), nor does it point to any anomalies in West Virginia’s voter registration data.
“Indeed, the letter contains the term ‘purpose’ but does not use the word ‘basis’” or provide any equivalent explanation supporting the necessity of the records request,” he wrote. 
West Virginia Secretary of State Kris Warner
In a statement, Secretary of State Kris Warner called the judge’s decision “an important victory for the rule of law, voter privacy, and the dedicated election officials across West Virginia who work every day to ensure the accuracy of our state’s voter registration system.”
“From the outset, my Office has maintained that West Virginia law prohibits the disclosure of sensitive personal information contained in the statewide voter registration system absent legal authority requiring its release,” Warner said. “Today’s ruling confirms that our position was well-founded and consistent with both our statutory obligations and our responsibility to protect the personal information of West Virginia’s registered voters.”
He added that his office shares the DOJ’s commitment to enforcing federal voter registration list-maintenance requirements and ensuring only eligible voters remain on the rolls. 
“Our disagreement has never been with that goal, but with the means sought in this instance, which would have required the disclosure of sensitive personal information in a manner prohibited by West Virginia law,” Warner said.
The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

name: VTDigger
title: No one struggling to pay rent can meet a $12,000 deductible
description:
The people designing health insurance plans have lost touch with a basic fact: For many Vermonters, healthcare is a luxury they can't afford.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  No one struggling to pay rent can meet a $12,000 deductible.
text:
Dear Editor,
I was glad to see that Blue Cross Blue Shield canceled its proposed “Vermont Basic” health plans. The debate over this proposal showed just how completely disconnected the people designing these plans and our healthcare system have become from the lives of ordinary Vermonters.
To call a plan with an $11,800 deductible before the insurance would bother to kick in an “affordable option” exists only in a policy fantasy bubble. An individual or a family struggling to pay rent, buy groceries and keep up with utility bills in our very high-cost, low-wage society doesn’t suddenly gain access to healthcare just because their monthly premium might drop by a few dollars. They simply trade one unaffordable bill for another.
When people face deductibles this large, they don’t shop for healthcare — another abomination of our high-cost culture — they avoid it altogether. They skip doctor’s visits, delay tests and ration medications until a minor problem becomes a medical crisis. That isn’t insurance. It’s medical roulette. 
The Green Mountain Care Board was definitely right to question whether these plans would provide real savings or simply shift more costs onto patients. But the larger problem is that we continue debating how to make inadequate insurance slightly less expensive instead of asking why and what we have done to make our healthcare so unaffordable in the first place.  

READ MORE

Too many healthcare decisions are made by people who never have to choose between paying the rent or seeing a doctor. Vermonters need affordable access to care through a universal publicly funded system, not the illusion of affordability created by lower premiums paired with crushing deductibles.
Until our policymakers and our so-called business leaders stop living inside this fantasy bubble and start listening to the people forced to live with these plans, healthcare will always look affordable in the executive suites and completely out of reach in real life.
Walter CarpenterMontpelier, Vt.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Caregiver issued a warning after nursing home resident chokes and dies
description: A nursing home worker accused of failing to evaluate a choking resident who subsequently died has been given a warning by state regulators. The Iowa Board of Nursing recently charged licensed practical nurse Samantha Smith of Burlington with failing to assess or evaluate a patient and committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s […]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing oversees nursing homes in the state of Iowa. (Photo via Getty Images; logo courtesy of the State of Iowa) A nursing home worker accused of failing to evaluate a choking resident who subsequently died has been given a warning by state regulators.
The Iowa Board of Nursing recently charged licensed practical nurse Samantha Smith of Burlington with failing to assess or evaluate a patient and committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare.
According to the board, Smith was employed last year as a nurse at the Klein Center, which is a nursing home that’s part of Southeast Iowa Regional Medical Center in West Burlington.
The board alleges that on Dec. 5, 2025, Smith responded to an incident involving a female resident of the home who appeared to be choking. State inspection reports indicate another resident of the home had alerted the staff to the fact that the woman had been coughing and vomiting while trying to eat.
The staff made note of the woman’s labored breathing and described her in their reports as choking, according to inspectors. The board alleges Smith failed to perform the necessary assessments of the woman’s vital signs and instead took her to her bedroom.
Smith then gathered the resident’s medications for the evening and allegedly placed the pills in the woman’s mouth and gave her water while the woman continued to cough and gag, eventually spitting out the pills, according to state inspectors.
The inspectors allege Smith then directed a certified nurse aide to put the woman to bed, after which Smith placed the woman’s CPAP mask in place, covering the woman’s mouth and nose, to help with the woman’s sleep apnea.
About 10:30 p.m., five hours after the choking episode in the dining room, the resident was checked by another nurse who discovered the woman was struggling to breathe and had vomited in her CPAP mask. According to state inspectors, the resident’s oxygen saturation levels were at 34% — with anything below 88% typically considered a medical emergency — and another nursing home worker reported overhearing the nurse exclaim, “Oh, my God.”
An ambulance was summoned, but the resident died before emergency services arrived at the nursing home, according to the board.
State inspectors later reported that when they asked the licensed practical nurse — identified in board records as Smith — whether she had performed “any assessments, like listening for lung sounds, vital signs or checking oxygen levels, (she) teared up and stated no.”
State inspectors proposed, but held in suspension, a $10,000 fine against the Klein Center. State fines are typically suspended in lieu of federal penalties imposed by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
The Iowa Board of Nursing recently settled its disciplinary case against Smith by issuing her a warning. As part of that settlement, Smith has agreed to complete 15 of educational training on patient assessments.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Smith for comment.

text:
Explore Delaware Schools combines official data and attendance maps, while First State Educate offers added context and parent connections
DOVER, Del. — Delaware families now have a new places to begin when searching for information about public schools, including attendance boundaries, school profiles and available performance data.
The Delaware Department of Education has launched Explore Delaware Schools, a public portal intended to bring information previously spread across multiple websites, reports and mapping tools into one location.
The website allows families to enter a home address to identify schools, review attendance boundaries, explore school profiles and connect with additional statewide education resources.
“Families deserve one trusted starting point to understand their public schools,” Secretary of Education Cindy Marten said. “Our responsibility is not simply to publish information. It is to make that information understandable, accessible and useful.”
The portal could be especially helpful for families enrolling a child in kindergarten, moving to a new community, considering school options or trying to understand which public school serves their neighborhood.
Its launch also addresses a longstanding challenge for Delaware parents: Basic school information has often been scattered among state reports, district websites, individual school pages and separate data systems.
The new portal is designed to serve as the state’s official front door for school information, providing families with access to school profiles, attendance boundaries, available performance information and interactive mapping tools.
However, finding official data is often only the first step.  First State Educate is expanding a different kind of portal.
Parents may also want to understand why a school’s performance is changing, how district decisions are made, what is happening at local school board meetings or how changes in funding, leadership, boundaries and academic programs could affect their children.
For families seeking that additional context, First State Educate’s Knowledge Hub can serve as a strong complement to the state portal.
First State Educate is an independent Delaware nonprofit focused on helping families understand and engage with the state’s public education system. Its Knowledge Hub provides parent-focused information about school governance, funding, accountability, school choice and education policy.
The organization can also connect parents with other families who share similar concerns, questions or experiences. Those connections can help parents compare information, learn how others have addressed similar challenges and identify opportunities to raise concerns collectively.
While Explore Delaware Schools supplies official state information, the Knowledge Hub can help parents interpret that information, understand the decisions occurring behind it and connect with others navigating similar issues.
The distinction is important.
The Department of Education remains the authoritative source for official school data, attendance boundaries and statewide reporting. First State Educate, as an education-focused nonprofit, can offer additional explanation, analysis and updates about developments within individual schools and districts.
The Knowledge Hub is intended to help families understand subjects such as how school boards operate, how education funding decisions are made, how to interpret school performance information and how policy changes may affect students.
Together, the two resources can provide families with a more complete picture.
Explore Delaware Schools can tell parents which school serves their address and provide available performance information. First State Educate can help explain what the information means, suggest questions parents may want to ask, connect them with other parents and help families become more involved.
District and individual school websites will also remain important sources for meeting agendas, staffing announcements, construction projects, program changes and day-to-day information affecting students.
No single website is likely to answer every question a family may have. But the launch of Explore Delaware Schools gives Delaware parents a clearer place to start, while First State Educate’s Knowledge Hub offers a way to dig deeper, understand changes and connect with others facing similar concerns.
“When people spend less time searching for answers, they spend more time making informed decisions for their children,” Marten said.

Best for: Finding schools by home address and reviewing official state information.
Website: explore.education.delaware.gov
First State Educate Knowledge Hub
What: A parent-focused resource offering explanations and context about school governance, funding, accountability, school choice and education policy.
Best for: Understanding what school data means, following decisions affecting Delaware schools and districts, and connecting with other parents who share similar concerns or questions, and more.
